#156640. Breaking: 7 Cars With The Smallest Trunks You Can Imagine

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1915 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 7 Cars With The Smallest Trunks You Can Imagine

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, no single car can deliver everything that every driver will ever want from it, and they all come with at least some compromises.
  • That doesn't make them inherently bad cars, they just excel in other areas.
  • It has been revealed that for this list, we've singled out seven cars with laughably small trunks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, no single car can deliver everything that every driver will ever want from it, and they all come with at least some compromises. Performance cars often aren't that fuel efficient, huge trucks and SUVs with impressive towing capabilities are not the most nimble for around town, and — as this list will prove — a variety of city and sports cars also need to compromise on trunk space, in order to prioritize other key traits.

That doesn't make them inherently bad cars, they just excel in other areas. The list includes various city-slick models like the Scion iQ and Renault Twizy – if these cars were equipped with cavernous trunks, then the smallest parking spots and tightest city streets would likely be best avoided. Similarly, sports and supercars, like the Fiat X1/9 and Audi R8 featured below, sport mid-engine layouts, which naturally make incorporating decent trunk space quite a tricky ordeal.

It has been revealed that for this list, we've singled out seven cars with laughably small trunks. If you know of smaller, feel free to drop them in the comments below, although it's probably important to point out that we've deliberately avoided models with zero trunk space — so, no BAC Mono or Morgan Plus 4 models to be found here. Likewise, not all trunk capacities are listed by automakers, so any models we could not reliably verify — such as the Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse's supposed 1.3-cubic-foot trunk — have also been avoided. With that aside, here is our selection of seven notoriously impractical trunks and the cars they belong to, listed in size order, with the largest featured first.

According to recent reports, the first entry is an Italian classic that does things differently. Whereas most mid-engine sports cars hailing from Italy boast impressive engines and lofty outputs, the Fiat X1/9 instead makes do with a tiny inline-4. It sports just a 1.3-liter capacity, and power peaks at 67 horses, with 68 pound-feet of torque for good measure. Even with a 2,200-pound curb weight, it still takes around 15 seconds for the little X1/9 to crack 60 mph from a standstill.

According to recent reports, as those figures suggest, this is a small car — its wheelbase is just 86.7 inches, which is over 4 inches shorter than that of the Miata below. As a result, there isn't a whole heap of room left for a considerable trunk — the X1/9's frunk provides owners just 5.1 cubic-feet of space.

However, here's where the X1/9 actually impresses, as, despite the diminutive proportions and mid-engine configuration, it actually manages to incorporate a traditional trunk, too. Here lies 4.1 cubic-feet of storage space, so in total, the tiny Fiat actually provides 9.2 cubes — very impressive, considering the space available in other mid-engine efforts. That frunk is typically used as stowage space for the removable targa roof panel, but, of course, with the roof in place or left at home, it could be used for whatever.

This list covers many city-centric little runabouts and exotic supercars, but here instead, we focus on something that lies somewhere between the two. Mazda's timeless MX-5 Miata is a back-to-basics sports car that refuses to follow the status-quo. While other sports cars have resorted to larger dimensions, heftier curb weights, turbocharged engines, and higher engine outputs, Mazda instead continues to focus on simple driving pleasures.

That's perfect for drivers chasing a fun drop-top to enjoy on a local back road, but it does mean that, once again, trunk space takes a back seat on the priorities list. At least, due to Mazda adopting a traditional front-engine and rear-wheel drive configuration, the Miata sports a proper trunk. It only offers 4.6 cubic-feet of actual space, though, so it's never going to be a great touring companion — at least not without owners having to make some sort of packing compromise or opting for an external luggage rack. The cabin isn't particularly clever in terms of extra storage either, with no door compartments to be seen and no traditional glove box.

It has been revealed that interestingly, the current ND-generation MX-5 Miata sports less luggage space than its predecessor, so Mazda clearly did not feel that trunk space had ever been much of a sticking point with Miata buyers in the past. In fact, we recently advised you all to buy a Miata and remarked that you'd likely never regret it, so we also feel the sports car's limited storage space is nothing too concerning either.

According to recent reports, lamborghini is the only automaker to appear twice on this list, although we doubt being called out for limited cargo space is going to damage the Italian supercar manufacturer's brand image all too much. The Temerario continues the baby supercar bloodline, following on from the Huracan and Gallardo before it, and unlike the Aventador-based Countach further down your page, it's an all-latest and fresh design.

There is a pattern emerging here, too, as much like the Countach revival, the Temerario is another mid-engine supercar, and another to sport hybridization technology. Naturally, that leaves no space for a traditional trunk, so it offers a frunk as its primary storage solution. It also matches the capability of later Audi R8 Coupe models, with only 4 cubic-feet of space given at the front end. That's perhaps enough for a few backpacks for a weekend getaway, but certainly not ideal for longer trips that may require multiple larger bags.

In a recent development, it doesn't matter how you spec a Temerario, it's never going to be a great grand-tourer with that little in the way of storage space. An Urus or front-engined model from another exotic brand would be the better bet there, but at least Lamborghini provides owners with enough space to stash away a few essentials for weekends away.

It has been revealed that audi had never made anything that truly verged on being a supercar, so when it pulled up in the late 2000s with a true 911 competitor, with a naturally aspirated and midship 4.2-liter V8, 6-speed manual, and quattro all-wheel drive, the motoring world sat up and paid attention. By all accounts, it was a sublime car, although, thanks to its mid-engine configuration, cargo space has always been at a premium.

Second-generation cars, which ran from the 2016 model year until Audi's supercar became one of the many nameplates that got the axe in 2024, came with a total of 8 cubic-feet of storage space behind the seats, while the physical frunk itself sports 4 cubic-feet. As for those first-gen models, the total frunk space matches that of the Toyota iQ, at only 3.5 cubic-feet. There is no mention of classifying the space behind seats as official stowage space here, so perhaps doing so was just a smart marketing trick of the later cars to make the R8 look like a more complete 911 rival. Either way, there is surely space for a pair of shades or a short novel in the cabin of first-gen models somewhere.

Moving back away from performance cars, the next entry on our list is another cleverly packaged city car. The Scion iQ, or Toyota iQ, as it was known in other markets, was a dinky little four-seater, the first four-seater, in fact, to sit at less than 3 meters (9.8 feet) in length, although it was certainly more conventional in its approach than the tandem-seat Twizy, detailed below. In truth, the Scion iQ was an excellent little car that nobody wanted to buy, produced from the 2012 through 2015 model years, and powered by a naturally aspirated 1.3-liter inline-4 engine.

It has been revealed that while it did have the capacity to seat four, those rear seats were particularly restrictive and better treated as an additional storage area. Just as well, as the designated storage space in the trunk was equally as restrictive, at just 3.5 cubic-feet. While the little city car certainly has its fans, not everyone loves it: Consumer Reports called it "slow, noisy, and uncomfortable," in addition to "less-than-enjoyable to drive.".

Recent findings suggest that still, it probably made good sense for those who commuted solely within packed city centers. Furthermore, if those buyers had far deeper pockets and wished for a more upscale ownership experience, they could always opt for the iQ's posher sibling, the Aston Martin Cygnet. The British luxury carmaker took the back-to-basics iQ, furnished it with a sublime interior and refinished the rear end, in addition to many other cosmetic and quality updates. It commanded around three times the price of the iQ, was never offered for sale in the U.S., and, although undoubtedly far nicer to sit in, it likely still made do with the same measly 3.5 cubic-feet of trunk space.

At the complete other end of the spectrum, cargo space isn't far removed from what the city-centric Scion iQ has to offer. To celebrate the initial 1971 release of its Countach, Lamborghini released a modern-day Countach built on the Aventador's chassis. A hybrid V12 powertrain pinched from the Sián FKP37 hybrid hypercar was selected as the motivator, and, as a tribute to the original prototype's LP-112 model designation, just 112 were assembled.

Cargo space likely was not at the forefront of the designer's mind, and neither was it a key priority for buyers either, we can safely assume, as the Countach LPI 800-4 offers just 2.2 cubic-feet of it. That's roughly enough room for two standard milk crates — great news for big milk drinkers, then, but not ideal for road trippers or those who fancy an exotic daily driver.

In a recent development, the Aventador Coupe, on which the Countach is based, manages to boast 5 cubic-feet of cargo space, so more than double, which might make the Countach's lack of available space seem tricky to understand. While Lamborghini (rightfully) doesn't feel the need to explain the Countach's cargo space, which is actually frunk space rather than trunk space, we can assume it's due to the Countach's differing lines and the fact it also boasts a hybrid system, whereas the Aventador is without electrification.

According to recent reports, the Renault Twizy was not sold in the U.S., as it likely wouldn't sell well being such a diminutive electrified city runabout, and restrictions would render it pretty difficult to use anyway. And that's if it ever worked its way around the required crash tests in the first place. Having said that, Scoot Networks did temporarily employ a fleet of them around San Francisco for rental use, but that's not why it grabs the spotlight today.

Recent findings suggest that instead, it impresses — or rather disappoints — with its ludicrously compact trunk capacity. It offers just 31 liters of space, which, for reference, works out to around 1.09 cubic-feet. To put that into perspective, a standard milk crate measures up at 0.9 cubic-feet. So, the Twizy is ideal for grabbing a few gallons of milk, but that's about it.

Industry observers note that in truth, it would be rude and missing the point somewhat to blast the Twizy over cargo space. It's designed to be as compact as possible, suitable for two occupants in tandem and, well, nothing else really. So, for city-center commuting and securing the last parking spot that nobody else dares to entertain, this quadricycle is absolutely ideal. Just be careful about the size of your packed lunch before heading out to work.

#156638. Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP).
  • The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets.
  • As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP). The program starts with Fresh York City apartment residents. I went to the RE+ in Las Vegas to meet with leaders from Jackery and Every Electric to learn more.

The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets. For the customer, the process is simple:.

Sources indicate that that’s it. As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery. Over the 11-year rated lifespan, purchasing the battery could increase the total net payback, although the upfront cost would be a little higher.

Industry observers note that it seems almost too simple and convenient for the customer. However, a lot of complex work and coordination is happening behind the scenes. The Jackery battery is in communication with Every Electric, who automates power management to charge when electricity demand is low and discharge to run the air conditioner when electricity demand is high. This kind of active demand response can go far beyond the typical TOU plan to directly mitigate utility demand shifts. Every Electric monitors data for each battery. The demand response of the combined storage across thousands of individual batteries is aggregated and sold to the utility, in this case Con Edison. Then the benefits are divided up and distributed to customers based on their contributions. Over 2000 batteries were in the initial trial phase, with a larger scale rollout planned next year. I am already on the waitlist, along with over 15,000 other NYC households.

Sources indicate that because it does not feed electricity back into the grid, implementation is much simpler. No electrician needed. The system monitors the amount of energy being stored and deployed at the point of use with no need for user intervention. Unlike traditional demand response that turns off appliances, there is no inconvenience to the user. Thermostats do not need to be adjusted. Smart appliances are not needed. The battery simply provides power when grid demand is high, shaving off the peaks.

You may still be asking “what’s the catch?” Right now, the system needs to coordinate a large number of relatively small batteries under the same utility to have enough combined capacity to sell to the utility. To start, it is only being offered in Latest York City, which sets the blueprint. In the initial application, the batteries will be used with 120V air conditioners, up to around 12,000 BTU. This is a common size for NYC apartments, letting one battery size serve a wide range of customers, simplifying initial rollout. It also offers clear return on investment based on how much electricity is used, when that electricity is used and when demand peaks for the utility. However, I wouldn’t expect it to stop there.

It has been revealed that the batteries being used are led by the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. This battery has 2042 Wh of capacity and up to 2200 W of output with 4400 W of surge power. A total of three outlets are on the front panel, as well as two USB-C and a USB-A port. Due to the UPS function, the portable power station adds protection and would be ideal to plug in a computer or sensitive electronics, in addition to the air conditioner. Although the VPP is based on air conditioner use, using all the outlets can potentially add to the amount of load shifted by the VPP and, as a result, increase the amount of payback for the customer. Plugging in other forms of energy consumption could also extend the benefit beyond the times of year when the air conditioner is being used.

Industry observers note that at 40% smaller and 34% lighter than the previous generation model, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 weighs 39.5 lb. That’s less than a 5-gallon water cooler bottle but less bulky to carry. Due to the plug and play nature, people changing apartments within the city can easily take it with them at 13.2” x 10.4” x 11.5”. Multiple levels of safety protections and a ruggedized portable design using automotive-grade LFP batteries ensure safe operation even if apartment occupants bump into it.

That portability also contributes to the emergency preparedness capability of the battery. For the months of the year when the air conditioning isn’t running, the battery could provide backup power for a refrigerator in a power outage, for example. Of course, Jackery also offers batteries specifically for refrigerators. Those batteries are not a part of the initial program… yet.

Recent findings suggest that this also gets to a limitation of the current program. To keep the program manageable as it scales up, only one size of battery in one use case is initially being offered. Right now, the biggest challenge is scaling up. Making it too complicated at the start would make scaling up more difficult. However, once the program reaches scale, more options can become available. Jackery also offers batteries with greater aesthetic appeal, like the slim FridgeGuard, which may be a better fit for the homes of some customers. As the program scales up, the applications have the potential to diversify.

Recent findings suggest that much of RE+ focused on supplying power and storage for data centers. While residential clean energy tax credits (25D) have been cut, data centers can still benefit from the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit that can add up with bonuses to cover half the cost of the project. With additional state and federal incentives piled on top, the majority of the cost of data center ESS can be covered by subsidies. With the heavily subsidized storage and large-scale contracts with the utility, data centers can access benefits not typically available to residential customers.

Industry observers note that however, the plug-in VPP changes the energy storage dynamic. People get credit for energy storage deployment at the point of use. AI technology, rather than just being a consumer of resources, is being used to automate the VPP system and let the benefits flow to more families. By starting with small window air conditioners, the system also tends to provide relief to people living in typically older apartments, rather than the sleek newly introduced high rises with multi-million-dollar apartments.

There is no need for home electrical upgrades. In fact, by taking some of the load off the circuit, the potential for my wife to trip the breaker from ironing in the living room while the TV and air conditioner are running on the same breaker is reduced. As the energy monitoring comes directly from the battery, it also isn’t dependent on smart meters.

For the system to have enough total capacity to sell to the utility, the plug-in VPP needs to connect thousands of batteries to provide multiple MWh of storage. This scale can easily be accomplished in urban areas. In addition, the value of the system will heavily depend on the local price of electricity and the variability in price. In NYC, electricity is significantly more expensive than in most of the US.

It has been revealed that latest York City apartments are a perfect starting place. While apartments tend to be far more energy efficient than detached houses and have lower net emissions overall, many of us living in apartments have traditionally felt a bit left out on clean tech. We don’t have roofs for rooftop panels. We typically do not have attached garages to place large permanent batteries or access to modify the electrical panel. If we do have the ability to make electrical modifications to the apartment, they can be prohibitively expensive in NYC. As such, a plug-in VPP is an exciting development for those of us living in apartments.

A plug-in VPP also makes the benefits of battery energy storage more accessible to urban areas. Often, there is not room for container-sized batteries. In places like Upcoming York City, the fire regulations are so strict, and the permitting is so complicated that large-scale BESS becomes exceedingly difficult to execute. Large-scale BESS, if approved, could take years to deploy.

Recent findings suggest that according to NREL, the national average full installed price of utility scale BESS was $334/kWh of capacity in 2024, with hardware making up roughly two thirds of the total. However, the cost would undoubtedly be higher in NYC. For comparison, the discounted Explorer 2000 v2 in this program (which avoids retail markup) comes in at $318.32/kWh, with no added permitting or installation cost. That is also significantly less than the installed cost of many home batteries used in traditional VPPs, like Tesla Powerwall. Once delivered, it can be online within minutes.

At the moment, plug-in VPP is the fastest, easiest and least expensive way to add battery capacity that shaves peak demand on urban grids in the US.

Industry observers note that as high draw usage like air conditioning increases, more stress is placed on the grid. Transformer and other electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades can be expensive. Having storage at the point of use reduces the amount of electricity that needs to flow through the grid during peak periods. As plug-in VPP is deployed more broadly, the benefits will be experienced more broadly. And CO2 emissions can drop in the process.

While the benefits of the program are already attractive, the initial program may just be the tip of the iceberg. In New York City, buildings over 25,000 square feet must reduce their greenhouse gas emissions under Local Law 97 (LL97). This includes many apartment complexes and offices. The deployment of batteries at the point of use has the potential to reduce emissions.

While the current batteries and air conditioners in the program are 120V, Jackery also makes batteries that are 240V. For appliances that have intermittent use but high draw, like heat pumps, hot water heaters, ranges, etc., 240V connections are often needed to provide the necessary power. The electrification of applications that were previously run on gas or fuel oil can greatly reduce building emissions. But many apartment buildings do not have 240V outlets available. However, larger Jackery models can charge on 120V, accumulate charge and discharge at 240V for intermittent use. There is potential for batteries to support the higher voltage electrification without expensive electrical upgrades while also providing VPP benefit. The math would have to work out and it hasn’t happened yet. But the potential is clearly there.

In a recent development, overall, the potential applications for this approach are massive. Already, I can see the potential to transform energy storage in NYC. In talking with Jackery and Every Electric, I started thinking about where the technology could go from here. Plug-in VPP could apply far beyond just Fresh York City. However, that is for a follow-up article.

Buick GSX Stage 1s Are Super Rare Muscle Cars, But They're Common Compared To Stage 2s

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you take a moment to think of some classic-era American muscle car brands, names like Chevrolet, Pontiac, and Dodge immediately come to mind, but "Buick" doesn't.
  • It has been revealed that the model responsible is the 1970 Buick GSX Stage 1.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, "Stage 1" was only part of the GSX's performance story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you take a moment to think of some classic-era American muscle car brands, names like Chevrolet, Pontiac, and Dodge immediately come to mind, but "Buick" doesn't. Buick occupies a market segment just under luxurious Cadillac within the GM hierarchy of automakers, making athleticism something most wouldn't associate the brand with. Regardless, the marque was responsible for building one of the most torque-happy muscle cars of the classic era, with 510 pound-feet of torque on tap alongside 360 horsepower.

It has been revealed that the model responsible is the 1970 Buick GSX Stage 1. At the time, the GSX was locked in direct battle with more well-known adversaries such as the Pontiac GTO and the Dodge Charger, but even when it was new, few knew about it. It was one of the rarest of muscle cars — only about 400 were produced in 1970. To boot, it became even rarer as time went on, with just 24 built in total for the 1972 model year.

Recent findings suggest that however, "Stage 1" was only part of the GSX's performance story. There was also the incredibly fabled "Stage 2" iteration. Only a couple of fully fledged examples were ever produced  — making it one of the rarest Buick muscle cars to ever grace the pavement.

If you fancied a hot Buick muscle car in 1970, you could simply pop down to the dealership and buy something like the GS 350 or GS 455. Your most desirable choice, however, would have been the flagship Buick GSX, carrying a sticker price of about $4,880. It boasted the poise and presence of a tried-and-true muscle car with its black striping and lack of chrome trim — something rarely seen in a Buick of the time. The Stage 1 package was offered for just $199, adding 10 horsepower and things like a higher compression ratio at 10.5:1 versus the GSX's standard 10.0:1, a more aggressive camshaft, and larger valves.

It has been revealed that if you took a walk back into the Buick dealer's parts department, though — and also happened to be a drag racer — you could build yourself an even more powerful GSX with Buick-bred components that were off the standard books. This marked the initiation method for procuring a Stage 2 kit, and it needed to be special-ordered through dealers, rather than from Buick itself. The package consisted of a litany of upgrades over the Stage 1 version. Because it wasn't available to the public at first, the Stage 2 upgrade went without an RPO code.

The Stage 2 kit carried things like an 11.0:1 compression ratio and 2-inch circular exhaust ports, allowing the engine to breathe much more efficiently. A gigantic Holley carburetor sporting an 850 cubic-foot-per-minute flow rate sat atop an Edelbrock intake manifold, and a set of high-strength forged pistons handled the engine's combustion.

Recent findings suggest that all told, the Stage 2 GSX was thought to have roughly 100 more horsepower than Stage 1 models. To test its Stage 2 creation, Buick drummed up a pair of GSX prototypes outfitted with the complete kit, one of which was sent to Doug Jones and Dave Benisek — a pair of drag racers — for some stress testing, with the duo managing to achieve quarter-mile times under 11.7 seconds at trap speeds nearing 130 mph. Jones and Benisek continued to race their prototypical Stage 2 GSX throughout the 1970s, going undefeated during the National Hot Rod Association's 1972 season.

Sources indicate that that very same year, Buick finally made the existence of its Stage 2 project public, letting regular customers special-order parts from the program. As for the rough number of Stage 2 kits built, it's thought to be just about 75 pairs, the vast majority of them produced in 1972. Sadly, looming changes to American emissions standards rendered the factory-sponsored Stage 2 program moot before it could get really off the ground.

In a recent development, 1972 was a pivotal year for the classic American muscle car. Horsepower outputs had dropped dramatically by that time, and the GSX Stage 1 was no exception. While the 1970 model boasted 360 ponies, the '72 GSX Stage 1 made just 270. Fitting, then, that Buick's Stage 2 GSX dream would effectively flame out that year — right around the time emissions standards and rising fuel costs began to render the classic American muscle car a thing of the past.

#156636. Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Europe’s industrial hydrogen plans have a buyer problem.
  • Sources indicate that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg.
  • According to recent reports, at a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe’s industrial hydrogen plans have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a new hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

Sources indicate that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

According to recent reports, at a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

Sources indicate that the mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

In a recent development, the International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

According to recent reports, my TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

European ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

Ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

According to recent reports, hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

The supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

Policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

Recent findings suggest that the EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

For lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

In a recent development, industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs.
  • Recent findings suggest that heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes.
  • “Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Recent findings suggest that heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the concern by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

In a recent development, HYDAC’s latest “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

According to recent reports, field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later revealed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another notable advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” mentioned Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”.

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

It has been revealed that for wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

Industry observers note that as fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

In a recent development, “HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”.

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Recent findings suggest that proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. Solar module manufacturer Thornova Solar and Nextpower, a provider of advanced solar tracker and structural solutions, marked a milestone in their growing strategic cooperation with the signing of a Master Supply Agreement (MSA).

In a recent development, the agreement, declared at RE+ 2026, further strengthens the collaboration between the two companies, combining Thornova Solar’s U.S.-made solar modules with Nextpower’s U.S.-manufactured steel frame technology. The expanded effort is designed to deliver increased domestic content opportunities and enhanced structural performance, providing greater value to customers developing utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects across the United States.

It has been revealed that according to the companies, integrating advanced steel frame solutions into selected Thornova Solar module series addresses two increasingly key priorities in the U.S. solar market: maximizing domestic content and improving module resilience under demanding environmental conditions.

The combined solution offers several key benefits:.

According to recent reports, the solution is particularly relevant for projects in demanding U.S. environments, including high-wind regions across the Midwest and Southeast, where structural reliability and long-term module performance are critical considerations.

In a recent development, “The signing of this Master Supply Agreement represents an notable step in strengthening our relationship with Nextpower and expanding the value we deliver to U.S. customers,” noted Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director of Thornova Solar. “By bringing together U.S.-made solar modules and domestically manufactured steel frame technology, we are helping our customers increase domestic content while benefiting from stronger, more resilient module solutions. This is exactly the kind of collaboration needed to advance a competitive U.S. solar manufacturing ecosystem.”.

Sources indicate that “We’re excited to deepen our strategic collaboration with Thornova and bring modules featuring Nextpower’s domestically manufactured steel frames to the U.S. market,” said Jenya Meydbray, vice president and general manager of Nextpower. “NX CoreFrame offers a significant opportunity to advance module strength and reliability, addressing industry challenges such as glass breakage and demanding environmental loads while delivering greater confidence to solar developers and owners.”.

According to recent reports, the MSA reflects the shared commitment of both companies to strengthening domestic manufacturing and delivering solutions that respond to the evolving technical and commercial requirements of the U.S. solar market.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
  • This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash.
  • Sources indicate that adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!

This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!

Sources indicate that adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!

This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).

According to recent reports, at this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.

According to recent reports, the ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.

Sources indicate that looking at the best sellers in several size categories, the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.

Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.

Considering that 56% of the latest SUVs introduced this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).

Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.

Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:.

Sources indicate that A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000). This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the new generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.

BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the fresh generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations. Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?

BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations, which was a 44% increase YoY and a new record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles at the moment having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.

In a recent development, things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its newly introduced baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations, the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….

Sources indicate that after the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s fresh land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.

Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?

Recent findings suggest that as for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!

Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the new generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.

Sources indicate that still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6, the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!

According to recent reports, A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also latest VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?

Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s latest baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be mentioned about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi SU7, which had around 10,500 deliveries in October. Then there’s also the BYD Yuan Plus, which, after a long cross through the desert, seems to be picking up steam again. It scored 11,658 registrations last month, a new year best.

According to recent reports, looking at the 2026 ranking, the podium remained the same, and unless something unexpected happens, it should stay as it is until the end of the year, with the small Geely repeating its 2025 win. That also means the Tesla Model Y will return to silver after getting bronze in 2025, and the BYD Song will get back onto the podium after a one-year absence.

Below the podium positions, though, there was some news. The BYD Yuan Up and Leapmotor A10 are surfing the B-segment wave and both climbed a position, to 5th and 6th, respectively.

If the BYD Yuan Up continues on its current record streak, then the small crossover could even aim to surpass the #4 FCB Ti7 before the year ends.

Still, with three subcompacts right now in the top 6 (Geely Xingyuan, BYD Yuan Up, and Leapmotor A10), small is hot right now, in China.

Elsewhere, the BYD Sealion 05 was up two positions, to 16th, while the Wuling Mini EV is hoping to bring tiny city cars back into the spotlight, and in October, it jumped two positions, ending the month in 13th….

Industry observers note that looking at the overall manufacturer ranking, it is a sea of red. Everyone is losing sales — big time. The exception is #5 Leapmotor (+31% YoY), while #8 Xiaomi (+3% YoY) and #10 Xpeng (+0%) are just hanging on.

So, now, not only are foreign OEMs suffering (Nissan was down 70% in October, Honda was down 51%), but even domestic ones are being affected by the EV shift.

Some may be asking, “But what about #9 Nevo and its 125% growth rate?” Well, it isn’t so much that they are winning sales, but they are effectively replacing the sales of their mother brand, Changan, which in October was only 19th after a 60% drop in sales YoY.

Looking at the auto brand ranking, BYD is firmly in the leadership position (17.2%), while runner-up Geely held to its 7.1% market share.

According to recent reports, rising 3rd placed Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) is fast approaching Geely. It wouldn’t be surprising if the startup brand became the newly introduced silver medalist in the final days of the year.

Sources indicate that one thing is for certain though — Leapmotor will win its first medal this year. The only question is the material that it will be made of….

Sources indicate that speaking of position changes, Tesla had a horrible month (4.4%, down from 4.9% in September), which allowed Wuling (4.6%) to climb one position in October, into 4th. At the end of the year, expect Tesla to keep the #4 position, as its December peak should help it surpass Wuling.

Looking at OEMs/automotive groups/alliances, BYD is leading with 21.9% share of the market, up 0.1% in October.

Meanwhile, Geely remained in second with 11.8% share. The multinational conglomerate has the runner-up spot secured.

Recent findings suggest that #3 SAIC was stable (8%) and remained firm in the last place on the podium, while #4 Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) remained on the rise. Will we see the startup challenge SAIC in 2027 for the 3rd spot?

#156629. Breaking: 2027 Audi Q7 And SQ7 Are, Like, Reeeeally Good

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2424 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 2027 Audi Q7 And SQ7 Are, Like, Reeeeally Good

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it may feel like the Audi Q7 has existed forever, and in the world of modern cars, it kinda has.
  • Sources indicate that luckily for Audi, the third-gen 2027 Q7 and its performance-focused SQ7 sibling are two fantastically compelling options for the luxury SUV buyer to consider.
  • Full disclosure: Audi wanted me to drive its redesigned Q7 and SQ7 so badly that it flew me to California's wine country, put me up in a swanky hotel, and kept me fed for a couple of nights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it may feel like the Audi Q7 has existed forever, and in the world of modern cars, it kinda has. The first-generation Audi Q7 debuted 20 years ago now, making a name for itself as a chicer and more car-like option among three-row luxury SUVs such as the Volvo XC90, Land Rover LR3, and Mercedes-Benz GL. The second-gen Q7 has been around for 10 years, and over its lifespan Ingolstadt's three-row SUV has faded into the background of the now much more competitive segment, so it's about time the Q7 got a good redesign.

Sources indicate that luckily for Audi, the third-gen 2027 Q7 and its performance-focused SQ7 sibling are two fantastically compelling options for the luxury SUV buyer to consider. If you need even more space than the Q7 offers, Audi also recently introduced the excellent fresh Q9 and SQ9, which thoroughly impressed me during my first drive review. My colleague Andy Kalmowitz accurately and eloquently described the Q9 as "a new-generation Q7 that took half a Viagra," so you'll see a lot of similar specs and conclusions in this review — like its longer sibling, the new Q7 is really damn good.

Full disclosure: Audi wanted me to drive its redesigned Q7 and SQ7 so badly that it flew me to California's wine country, put me up in a swanky hotel, and kept me fed for a couple of nights.

It has been revealed that the third-generation Audi Q7 is 199.1 inches long, only 0.2 inches shorter than the outgoing model, but the new Q7 is 2.7 inches taller and 1.5 inches wider. Interior dimensions have only changed slightly as well, with the new one offering slightly more cargo space and second-row legroom, but slightly less front seat headroom and third-row legroom on paper. This all varies, though, since the second row of seats slide forward and back to allow for the best combination of space for your family's unique needs.

In a recent development, in standard Q7 form the SUV is powered by a twin-turbocharged 2.9-liter V6 that sends 429 horsepower and 442 pound-feet of torque through a slick-shifting eight-speed automatic transmission. From there, naturally, the power goes to all four wheels through a upcoming Quattro all-wheel-drive system with a limited-slip center differential. This standard powertrain is capable of a 0-to-60 time of 4.8 seconds, which Audi claims is the quickest in the segment, and in practice it's plenty powerful. That's a lot of standard performance baked into the Q7's base price of $72,295.

There's also a lot of luxurious features included as standard at that price, including an opening panoramic sunroof, 14-way power front sports seats with four-way lumbar and memory, Audi's array of three screens, LED lights with three different daytime running light designs, natural wood inlays, three-zone automatic climate control, a power tailgate, power-folding third-row seats, a surround-view camera system, and leather upholstery.

My test car was a top-trim Q7 Prestige with a price of $91,435, which included the 21-inch wheel package, the 4D audio system, a trailer hitch, and second-row captains chairs.

The SQ7, like the SQ9, is powered by a reworked twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 that sends 591 horsepower and 590 lb-ft of torque through an eight-speed automatic transmission to a new rear-biased Quattro system with an electronically locking rear differential. If that sounds like a lot of power to you, you're wrong. I think it's the perfect amount of power for a three-row family SUV, and it's a valuable safety feature to be able to complete the 0-to-60 sprint in an Audi-claimed 3.7 seconds. You know, just in case.

All that power comes with a base price of $100,095, but that includes some features that are only found on upper trim levels of the Q7, including Audi's upcoming hands-free highway driving assistant, a Bang & Olufsen 3D stereo, Nappa leather ventilated and massaging front seats, adaptive air suspension, all-wheel steering, and heated outboard second-row seats.

Like the Q9, both of these smaller SUVs can also be optioned with a Luxury package that includes automatic doors, digital OLED tail lights, eight digital DRL signatures, and an illuminated grille to luxe things up. Both are also offered with Audi's Digital Matrix LED headlights that are finally allowed in the U.S.; these will allow drivers to leave their high beams active while the car identifies and selectively dims some of the lighting elements in order to prevent blinding other cars, and it blocks the beam from hitting street signs that could reflect the beam and dazzle the driver. My test car was a decked-out SQ7 with the 23-inch wheel package, 4D audio, a trailer hitch, second-row captain's chairs, and the Luxury, Executive, Vision, and S Sport packages. It had a total price of $117,085.

It has been revealed that during my drive on the winding roads around California's wine country, through the redwood forests and along the rocky northern coast, the upcoming Q7 and SQ7 revealed themselves as excellent luxury SUVs. The Q7's base powertrain, if you can call it base, was more than punchy enough to get the nearly 5,200-pound three-row SUV up to freeway speeds lickety-split. Audi's 4.8-second 0-to-60 claim felt almost like an underestimation to the butts of myself and my co-driver, and that estimation is also 0.7 seconds quicker than the outgoing V6-powered Q7, so there's a lot of extra shove hiding under the more upright hood of the new car.

It has been revealed that activating launch control unlocks the most exhilarating acceleration, and it's easily done. Just press the traction control button once and tap the shifter down to engage S mode, then stomp on the brake pedal, floor the gas, and release the brakes.

Sources indicate that twisty roads may not appeal to most three-row SUV drivers, but they will be a delight to anyone who drives a new Audi Q7 because it is one well sorted driving machine. Whether in the default Balanced drive mode or the zestiest Dynamic mode, the Q7 was not just capable but felt happy to dance through the damp curves and swerves that wound us through the downright verdant Redwoods State Park and along the breathtaking cliffs of Cape Horn.

Sources indicate that some of the credit for my test Q7's excellent driving dynamics must go to its top-tier Prestige trim level, which equips the Q7 with one of the most natural feeling and effective all-wheel-steering systems I've ever experienced. It made the Q7 feel significantly more agile than its girth leads one to believe when getting frisky in the twisties, and it made low-speed maneuvering a breeze, even in the tight, small-town parking lots of Ukiah, California.

The Q7 Prestige trim also includes front sport seats with power adjustable bolsters, which provided prestigious levels of comfort over the course of my seven-hour long drive day. They're actually the same seats that come standard on all SQ7s, and they also happen to have one of the most effective massage functions of any car on the road.

Industry observers note that as a whole, the Q7 provided an experience that was befitting of a $90,000 luxury SUV, with exceptional comfort, a stress-free driving experience, and a smooth and gutsy powertrain. The only two demerits that could potentially put luxury buyers off are a taut ride quality that doesn't isolate passengers from roadway imperfections quite as much as other comfier SUVs, and a bit more road noise than some competitors. Both of those factors could have been down to the large wheels and tires on my test car, though.

It has been revealed that much the same as its bigger SQ9 sibling, the SQ7 is mind-bendingly quick and adept at bombing down a back road. The SQ7's twin-turbo V8 sounds fantastic from both outside and inside the cabin, where its deep bellow and occasional off-throttle burbles were just loud enough to put a devious smirk on my face without being intrusive or overbearing.

My test car was fully loaded, including the $1,200 S Sport air suspension that also gets you racy red-painted brake calipers, and the setup was paired with the $2,500 23-inch wheels that are shroud in 285/35 front and 315/30 rear Hankook Ventus evo SUV summer performance tires, which look downright sick but likely contributed to the stiffer ride.

The S Sport air suspension felt a bit chattery over broken pavement in Balanced mode, and that slight chatter was amplified in Dynamic mode. Over a few particularly bumpy spots, Dynamic mode's suspension tuning made the SQ7 feel like a pebble skipping across the surface of a lake, so I kept it in Balanced mode, which was already firm enough. The steering wasn't overly communicative, but it was exceedingly direct without feeling frantic or darty, and I was still able to ascertain when the front tires were beginning to lose their fight with the laws of physics.

Despite the overly stiff suspension, I was utterly floored by the way the entire package came together to make a 5,500-pound SUV handle like it was on rails, a journalist cliché that is apt here. My co-driver was a self-proclaimed "coaster head," and he stated the SQ7 really felt like a roller coaster when I was driving very sensibly down a tantalizingly rolling and winding road.

It has been revealed that it also elicited a similar response when we found space to put Audi's 3.7-second 0-to-60 claim to the test and do a few launches. It's a good idea to secure any loose items in the vehicle before you activate launch control, because they'll rapidly become high-speed projectiles as the SQ7 shoves its occupants into the quilted leather thrones with dizzying force until the driver chickens out and lifts their right foot. It launches with the ferocity of an EV, but with all the good old fashioned drama that comes with several thousands of precisely timed explosions per minute and an occasional muscular kick from a gear change. It rocked — and it sucked gas. The trip odometer showed a dismal 12.5 mpg after my three-hour drive that mixed highway and a fair amount of admittedly intense backroad blasting, so it's no gas saver.

In a recent development, I'm sure you're tired of hearing me talk about how great the upcoming Q7 and SQ7 are by now, and though they are both truly top tier vehicles, there are some little faults. The Q7 is still a sort of 'tweener model that straddles the midsize and full size classes; Audi reps described it as a do-it-all model that offers a small family the option to occasionally tote around three rows worth of children, but not it's necessarily meant for full-time three-row duties. I'd concur with that assessment, since it was difficult to squeeze past the second-row captain's chairs to climb into the third row, and once I got back there I realized the seat bottoms sit virtually on the floor of the car, so I ended up in an upright fetal position. The Q7's third row is still best suited for smaller humans with youthful joints.

In a recent development, both of the cars I drove were optioned with the second-row captain's chairs, which look fantastic and are respectably comfortable, but there is no way to option ventilated second-row seats, and the seats did not recline far enough for true long-distance comfort. I sat in the second row of a Q7 for the two-hour drives from the airport to the hotel and vice versa, and I kept checking to make sure the seat backs didn't recline any further because I could not believe how limited their recline was. Second-row legroom was reasonable, but if the front seats were scooted back too far, it impinged upon the second-row space more than one may expect from such a large vehicle. I'm 6-foot-8 and mostly legs, so I'm definitely an outlier, but I try to think about more reasonable body shapes and sizes as well, and I still think the Q7's second row isn't as spacious as it could be.

It must be noted that things looked and felt fantastic inside the Q7 and SQ7, with leather covering the entire door cards down to the generously sized door bins that easily accommodated my oversized Emotional Support Water Bottle. The use of black plastic trim has been kept to a minimum, aside from the giant bezels that surround the strangely shaped touchscreen arrangement, and I'm happy to report that the Q7's interior felt as solid, high-quality, and luxurious as an Audi ought to. The same goes for the materials in the second row, which isn't as common, and even the Q7's rear doors bring the leather all the way down to the door bins.

In a recent development, the Q7 uses Audi's current array of screens, and unfortunately that means there are no physical climate controls and not even any physical air vent adjustments — everything has to be done through the touchscreen. This shouldn't pose too significant of an problem for owners, since they will likely set their preferences and save them to their driver profile or the seat memory settings, but I'll never prefer adjusting my air vents through a touchscreen over a simple physical toggle.

The standard passenger screen is gimmicky to me, and anyone who read my Q9 or Mercedes-Benz GLE review will know that I hate when the passenger screen doesn't include passenger-specific controls. For example, the sport seats in my test cars all had adjustable side bolsters and thigh support, but the only way to adjust those functions was through the center infotainment screen. The passenger screen did incorporate controls for the passenger's massage settings, but forcing the passenger to reach across the dashboard and commandeer the entire center infotainment screen just to make a simple seat adjustment was infuriating. Plus, the infotainment screen is rather dramatically aimed at the driver, so it can be difficult to see and navigate from the passenger seat.

Beyond those gripes, though, the Q7 and SQ7 are exceptionally good midsize three-row luxury SUVs. In fact, I think they might be the most compelling cars in their segment, though I have yet to experience the new BMW X5. Some of Audi's recently revised products haven't exactly embodied the chic, stylish, and high-quality attributes that Audi's greatest models once did, but the Q7 and SQ7 are a return to form. They're stylish, well-priced, luxurious, solid-feeling, and exhilarating to drive, so I have to give it to the Ingolstadt team — they've outdone themselves on the new Q7.
