#156624. At $22,000, Is This 2006 BMW E46 M3 The Gold Standard?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

At $22,000, Is This 2006 BMW E46 M3 The Gold Standard?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, with every generation, BMW has made the M3 (and later M4) better.
  • Recent findings suggest that it is, of course, perfectly okay to be average.
  • According to recent reports, at first glance, the 2002 Honda CR-V EX AWD we looked at last Friday seemed pretty average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with every generation, BMW has made the M3 (and later M4) better. Today's Nice Price or No Dice E46 might be the baby bear "just right" edition, since it's "not too slow" and "not too complicated." Let's see if its price tag proves likewise.

Recent findings suggest that it is, of course, perfectly okay to be average. That is, after all, what most of us in the world are. It's a statistical reality required to define outliers to the norm. Or something like that. It's been a long time since I took either algebra or stats.

According to recent reports, at first glance, the 2002 Honda CR-V EX AWD we looked at last Friday seemed pretty average. CR-Vs are ubiquitous on the road, and our car wasn't growing a third arm off its roof or practicing freaky Looksmaxing in any way. What made the Honda above average in interest came down to two factors. First, it had a five-speed manual gearbox, a rarity on the model. The second was that while it had crazy high (241K) mileage, its owners had cared enough to keep it on the road to the point of going to the expense of fitting it with a lower-mileage engine. At $4,000, it was also priced right in the middle: not suspiciously low to trigger spidey senses that it might be a scam, nor so high as to make interested parties think the seller lives in an alternate reality. Ultimately, that resolved into a 77% 'Nice Price' win.

Few car companies exemplify the idea of overachievement better than BMW. Rising from borrowed microcar obscurity out of the ashes of WWII, the Bavarian brand built a reputation for sporting saloons and coupes. So successful was the effort that by the early 1970s the company's cars were considered benchmarks, with capable competitors like Datsun's 510 measured against the marque and described as "the poor man's BMW.".

Industry observers note that no model better exemplifies BMW's achievements as a marque than the M3. Along with the M5, the 3 Series-based sports car introduced the company's in-house motorsports division and a badge that quickly became inspirational to many enthusiasts.

The 2006 BMW M3 coupe we're looking at today represents what is arguably the pinnacle of M3-ness. No, it's not the most capable, highest-powered, or most technologically advanced in the line. What it is, though, is one of the last of the almost purely analog cars, and this one is kitted for the kind of driver that seeks out slinky bends, not slothful boulevards.

It has been revealed that first off, this M3 rolls double sixes. That's the 333-horsepower 3.2-liter S54 straight-six under the hood and the Getrag 420G six-speed stick that backs it up. Together, they have powered this M3 to a mere 55,732 miles, according to the ad. That works out to just under 2,800 miles a year.

Sources indicate that confusingly, the ad runs under the "For Sale by Owner" section of Craigslist, although the pictures imply that it's dealer-offered. That, or the current owner lives in a commercial-style space with an NA Miata parked in the living room.

It has been revealed that regardless, the ad doesn't give us much to go on regarding the car's condition, maintenance history, or whether it's spent its entire existence doing donuts in parking lots. All we get instead is the descriptor that the car "Runs great." As Craigslist listings require, we are also told the car has a clean title, so there's that. A PPI by a qualified BMW wrench-turner would be recommended for any interested party.

The pictures do tell a story, though. It shows the car to be painted in Phoenix Yellow, a fairly rare color and one that stands out from the crowd. Underneath the expressive hue, the bodywork appears to be in perfect condition, with no obvious dings, scrapes, or missing pieces. One odd choice appears to be the capping of the side marker lights on the front bumper, though that seems to be something M3 owners like to do, if the Internet is any indication. Underneath all that, the car wears Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys. Again, no word is given on the age or condition of the tires wrapping those.

The cabin is remarkable for being so unremarkable. Some natural creasing and buffing is evident on the driver's seat side bolster, but that's the cost of doing business in any car with cosseting seats. Nicely, however, there's no evidence of greasy mitts on the Alcantara steering wheel or leather shift knob. Everything is gloriously stock in here, right down to BMW's somewhat cryptic stereo and climate controls. Someone has also done an excellent job of vacuum-striping the floor mats, which is very zen and satisfying to see.

As noted, the seller is frustratingly brief in the ad's description. Oddly, they do say that prospective tire-kickers "Must provide own transportation." Do they imagine people expect to be picked up at the airport and brought to see the M3, like the seller is running a livery service as a side hustle? Who knows. Besides, we need to focus on this BMW's $22,000 asking price. Yes, that amount will get you a slightly used Kia with some warranty left; what's your point?

It has been revealed that what do you say, is this clean and capable E46 M3 worth that $22,000 asking despite the info-light ad description and the requirement of arranging your own transportation to simply view it? Or is that too much to ask for an ad that says so little?

Boston, Massachusetts, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#156621. Breaking: 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA EV Is A Semi-Charmed Kind Of SUV

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2123 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA EV Is A Semi-Charmed Kind Of SUV

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that driving a 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA won't make your nostalgic radio station jam session sound sweeter, though the 16-speaker Burmester surround sound system is very good.
  • Recent findings suggest that mercedes had a few journalists out to Spain to drive the 2028 GLA250+ and GLA350 in their pure EV forms.
  • Full disclosure: Mercedes-Benz paid for me to fly to Spain, set me loose on the Spanish countryside in two fully charged GLAs, kept me fed and put me up in a hotel for two nights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that driving a 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA won't make your nostalgic radio station jam session sound sweeter, though the 16-speaker Burmester surround sound system is very good. Collective Soul, your friend of nearly 14 years and yourself won't harmonize any better. What the third-generation GLA will do, however, is provide a frictionless, airy and easy vessel for making memories in the sun. Turn up the volume using the haptic volume knob, turn on your fixed glass panoramic roof, and heaven, let your light shine down.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes had a few journalists out to Spain to drive the 2028 GLA250+ and GLA350 in their pure EV forms. Taking a ride up the Spanish coast in a car with a glass roof is a pretty fantastic way to spend a day. I only wished I was driving a convertible along the brilliant Spanish coast once (OK, maybe twice) during the whole drive thanks to a wide open airy cabin and whisper-quiet interior. This is a workhorse of an EV, not a pleasure cruiser, and when we got down to brass tacks it was clear there is still some work to be done.

Full disclosure: Mercedes-Benz paid for me to fly to Spain, set me loose on the Spanish countryside in two fully charged GLAs, kept me fed and put me up in a hotel for two nights.

Recent findings suggest that this is Mercedes-Benz's subcompact SUV, though this third-gen GLA is anything but sub or compact, having grown in every direction and stretching what it means to be a part of this category. The outgoing GLA has been on the roster since 2019, and Mercedes is hoping to give the GLA a shot in the arm with this new, more sporty design. It can be had with either hybrid or fully electric powertrains, the latter coming in single-motor, rear-wheel-drive GLA250+ and dual-motor, all-wheel drive GLA350 forms, mirroring the CLA and GLB it shares its platform with. Both have an 85-kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack that can be DC fast-charged at up to 320 kW, taking it from 10% to 80% in just 22 minutes, and a DC converter means it can be charged at both 800-volt and 400-volt stations. Drivers can adjust the regenerative braking via paddles on the back of the steering wheel. The settings range from hardly any at all, to a gentle tug, to an abrupt, lurching bite at its highest setting that I would think would be impossible to live with unless you were a real weirdo about range-maxxing.

The GLA250+ was the first tester I took out along the Spanish coast, and it was a genuine hoot. The winding roads were sharp and unfamiliar, but the GLA was sure-footed, whipping into the curves easily and handily. Normally, an EV drive on curvy roads would send my sensitive stomach into upheaval, but not in the GLA. My gut is rarely wrong about such things. The motor on its rear axle makes 268 horsepower and 247 pound-feet of torque, and it offers a range of up to 408 miles on the European WLTP cycle, which should translate to the mid-300s when the EPA gets its hands on it. The GLA250 is an everything car, from parking easily in the city to doing long road trips in serious comfort and commuting on the freeways with that nice EV torque surge for handy merging.

Recent findings suggest that that was not the case with the GLA350. Its pair of motors put out 349 hp and 380 lb-ft, enough to hit 60 mph from a standstill in 5.3 seconds (almost two seconds quicker than the GLA250), and the car just doesn't need the extra punch of power. What had been a relaxing drive up the stunning Spanish coast in the GLA250+ was punctuated by over-torqued jumps from dead stop. It just didn't make for a good driving experience. One motor and rear-wheel drive is really all you need. The range loss for the 4Matic model makes it extra not worth it, but the driving dynamics are enough to make me opt for the less powerful version.

The hybrid will come to our shores late next year after the EV, with a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine mated to a 48-volt lithium-ion battery and a small electric motor. When driving conditions require less than 30 hp, the electric motor takes over most of the momentum, adding its extra oomph to the gas engine at higher speeds.

Industry observers note that one thing Mercedes-Benz made clear to us journalists is that the new GLA is substantial. Every one of the GLA's measurements has grown compared to the outgoing model, including the wheelbase that has been stretched by 2.4 inches to 109.8 inches. It's six inches longer overall, too. At this rate, the next generation of GLA will be merely a compact SUV.

The front seats are comfortable and cushy, but the heating and massage elements aren't much to write a blog about. I might be a bad judge here, though, because I need to cook like a two-day-old 7/11 taquito in my car seat. The massage with heat option felt less like relaxing and more like I accidentally sat on someone with a bad fever and they were weakly poking me to alert me of my mistake. Unsettled, I turned it off.

It has been revealed that rear passengers get a whole inch and a half of extra legroom, and max headroom for front seat passengers grew almost an inch. Do these measurements seem like things you normally worry about in a car? Maybe not, but the overall effect works. The space in the back made me think this SUV would be great for parents of older kids, or childless folks who want to bring friends on trips but don't want to make them suffer a stuffy back seat. The back didn't strike me as particularly car-seat ready, though, and while the upcoming GLA does have a small frunk, the general storage situation would be tough with most younger kids. My prediction: the GLA won't baby all that well.

Recent findings suggest that is it a bit blob shaped? Yes. Is that the general shape of a lot of SUVs now for incredibly notable, crash-worthy, life-saving reasons? Also yes. I'm down with the blob, just give us some cool colors. Sadly, Mercedes does not give us many cool colors. There's red, blue, five shades of gray, and a new greenish gray called Liquid Crystal Green.

In a recent development, of course, it wouldn't be a new car without a blackout package, with Mercedes' Night package being offered alongside a matte black paint job. The GLA is also available with the AMG Line appearance package, which adds inches to your wheels and sporty elements to the interior, like stainless steel sport pedals and AMG sport seats. The AMG Line also comes with bright red seatbelts, which adds a much-needed pop of color to the interior, though sometimes it felt like a teacher trying to make safety fun for the class. 18-inch wheels are standard, but they can be bumped up to 19s or 20s.

Mercedes-Benz states it is aiming for a "welcome home" feel when folks enter their cars. There's a real lack of rescue pit bull nose prints on the glass for it to feel homey to me, but maybe for a classier breed of person who owns a classier breed of dog that rings true. The smoked-glass-effect Iconic grille on this beefy SUV does remind me of the nose of an exuberant puppy. Thanks to the additional height on the GLA, the upcoming grille doesn't overwhelm the front fascia to the same degree as on the C-Class EV. The lights embedded inside the glass grille give it a more jeweled appearance during the day than the black empty space of the last ICE generation. At night, 608 backlit polycarbonate lights turn the grille into a stunning display. A bunch of little lights always recalls celebrations like Christmas or bonfire nights, so the "Welcome Home" effect Mercedes is looking for snagged me there.

The MBUX AI Assistant still sucks. It's still a pain to turn off, it's still listening constantly, and it's still interrupting conversations unprompted or at the mere hint of its makers' name, something bandied about quite a lot by two journalists driving its car. When called upon to do the parlor trick of finding a specific alternative rock song or find a restaurant with dietary needs, it was often flumoxxed or demanded a log-in to some kind of account. Asking indirectly for information on a song, however, I got an interesting Pop-Up Videos–style spiel about the song and the car then asked "Would you like me to play it?" A radio station based on that song followed afterwards.

Recent findings suggest that last time I faced down the AI Assistant in the C-Class, it questioned my grip on my emotions because I was singing fairly tame Mountain Goats tunes (seriously, it wasn't even a tune about lunar cannibalism). At least on this drive it didn't try to direct me towards a domestic violence shelter for singing along to "Better Man" by Pearl Jam. Mercedes indicates its AI Assistant is an amalgamation of the best bits of ChatGPT, Google and Microsoft's large language models. If this is the peak, color me unimpressed. The average non-tech person either thinks LLMs are a neat trick, or they loathe it entirely. Mercedes would do well to make this feature a little easier to switch off.

Recent findings suggest that gang, I may be suffering from screen fatigue. Between phones, laptops for work and car interiors, it feels like I'm always numbly poking at an unfeeling pane of glass. There's a metaphor for life in there somewhere. The GLA comes with the dash and infotainment-swallowing giant screens surrounded by easily smudged piano black bezel, and this layout is feeling less luxurious by the day. Luxury should have more heft to it, more of a solid haptic feedback than crisp displays on top of crisp displays. Screens have gone from "this car is like a spaceship" to "this car is just like every other car on the road." That just ain't luxury, jack.

It has been revealed that case in point — I went to crank up the volume on the steering wheel to properly honor a Third Eye Blind song, and was thrilled to find the old roller volume knob right where I needed it on the steering wheel, but the control felt cheap and plasticky. Ditto on the weird whale tail–shaped window switches. Still, I'd take plastic bobbles for stuff like the HVAC and seat heating over navigating through touchscreen menu after touchscreen menu or turning to my long-time nemesis, the MBUX AI assistant. Turning off the AI, for instance, became a flurry of navigating touchscreens until my drive partner and I gave up after several attempts, and if there's one thing we journos know, it's how to mess with the settings. On either side of the screen are Mercedes' circular climate control air vents, which are also showing their age. Every time I see them I make the "Virtual Insanity" music video joke. Both the joke and design are well past their prime.

Then, there's the much-lauded passenger screen. I realize I sound like a cranky old woman complaining about luxury automakers these days with their screens and AI Assistants and corny interior lighting accents (yeah, I dislike those too), and maybe there are some folks out there who like to just ride along up front with the driver in their own little worlds, but tuning out to the point you're watching a whole show on your own 14-inch infotainment screen? Feels a bit rude and isolating, like having a loud phone conversation while trapped in an elevator with someone. This isn't a car to be chauffeured in, it's for families and friends and people who supposedly like each other. If you're on a long trip and need to tune out for a bit, that's what we have phones for.

In a recent development, the entire effect is a solid car with a lot of nonsense that makes it seem like Mercedes might be chasing trends rather than leading by example in the luxury market. Those blank, black bezeled areas between screens are a bleak reminder of where the thoughtful luxury used to go. Maybe I'm being too critical, but as an entry-level vehicle you have to hope it will set up buyers for a lifetime of returning to Mercedes-Benz and I am not sure seizing on the latest technological fads moves that goal post any closer for the brand.

Industry News: Memo To Musk: Denial Is Just The First Step On The Long Road To Recovery

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement.
  • In a recent development, during an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024.
  • In a recent development, in the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement. If Musk intends to stage a sort of political recovery, he still has a long way to go. Denial is just a precursor to recovery, which begins in earnest when you stop denying the reality of your situation and start admitting you need help from a higher power or some such. And in fact, a higher power is coming for Musk —  if not in spiritual form, then in the form of Congress, where the incoming Democratic majority plans to exercise its authority, and call Musk to account for manipulating SpaceX satellite services in Ukraine.

In a recent development, during an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024. Musk simply said he “felt foolish” for wasting his money on losers.

In a recent development, in the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014. Justin sayin’….

For those of you wondering why Elon Musk’s politics should be a matter of concern to CleanTechnica, that’s a good question, and here’s the answer: Elon Musk sailed into clean tech history on the coattails of the EV startup Tesla Motors (soon to become simply Tesla) in the early 2000’s, only to emerge in more recent years as a champion of the far right alongside President Donald Trump’s notoriously racist, fossil fuel-supporting “Make America Great Again” movement, thereby setting back the US decarbonization movement by years if not decades.

Musk has also made his own contribution to the resurgence of fossil fuels in the US. His new xAI data centers are well known for deploying loosely regulated (or illegal) on-site gas generators, and his SpaceX venture has been gobbling up natural gas for rocket fuel while laying plans for future expansion.

So much for Elon Musk’s footprint on the US energy profile. Let’s move over to Ukraine, where rich fossil energy and mineral resources in the nation’s Donbas region prompted Russian President Putin to send unmarked soldiers — aka the “little green men” — to annex that portion of Ukraine in 2014 (see clarification/correction below). A ceasefire temporarily calmed the situation until February of 2022, when Putin sent a fully equipped convoy to the Ukrainian capital city Kyiv, aiming to take over the entire seat of government in one fell swoop — literally, in one day.

The effort failed, both militarily and in terms of Putin’s energy goals. Ukraine promptly cut Russia off from its electricity grid and hooked up with the European grid, a complex effort assisted by the Biden administration. Ukraine also set the wheels in motion to join the European Union as a significant source of clean energy, including green hydrogen gas alongside its copious potential for clean power including biomass, wind, and solar power.

To put that into perspective, consider that Ukraine is almost 90% as large as Texas, which has staked out a leadership position in wind and solar power among the 50 US states.

With Ukraine as a leading renewable energy supplier, the EU would have a fresh opportunity to meets its decarbonization goals on schedule while also reducing imports of fossil energy from Russia… And… Well… That’s where Elon Musk enters the picture.

Musk first emerged as a full blown MAGA supporter in 2020, when he helped Trump stir up conspiracy theories and confusion over the federal response to the COVID-19 crisis, in a failed effort to support the President’s bid for re-election that year. Had Trump won, he would have continued to implement a key part of his foreign policy agenda, namely, withdrawing the US from NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance. NATO formed in 1949 as an effort to curb Russian expansion in Europe, an effort Trump has upended on account of his longstanding friendship with Putin.

The election of Joe Biden in 2020 did not prevent Musk from providing additional aid and comfort to Trump. Musk used his media-grabbing public profile to undercut the authority of President Biden at every opportunity, including on the world stage as well as here at home. The stream of insults extended into January of 2022, even as the reality of a fresh round of Russian expansion into Europe began to materialize.

Musk had an additional opportunity to challenge Biden’s authority in January of 2022, when the so-called “Freedom Convoy” of truckers barricaded government offices in Canada, ostensibly in protest of a vaccine mandate. Musk gleefully cheered the effort, which disrupted transportation systems and distracted public attention in two key NATO allies — Canada and the US — even as Russia began ratcheting up its plans to take over Kyiv.

According to recent reports, however, once it became clear that Putin’s one-day takeover of Ukraine was a failure, Musk about-faced. He took credit for providing “free” communications aid to Ukraine in the form of satellite services through the Starlink branch of SpaceX.

JK! A later assessment revealed that other sources shouldered about 85% of the cost of Starlink terminals initially supplied to Ukraine, including USAID here in the US (not a typo — that’s the US Administration for International Development, the same agency that Musk later destroyed in 2025).

Poland and other groups also contributed initial assistance to purchase  the terminals alongside an estimated 30% of connectivity costs. In addition, by September of 2022 Musk was making the case for US taxpayers to foot the bill.

Sources indicate that don’t just take my word for it. In 2023, the Belfer Center for International Affairs at Harvard recapped SpaceX’s negotiations over payment for its services to Ukraine during the previous year, concluding that “we can assume the U.S. government agreed to pay some, if not all, of the costs for continued operation of the technology.”.

“SpaceX, and particularly Musk, was able to play the role of wartime hero, showcasing the power and value of the technology products the firm developed, while simultaneously avoiding sustained and hefty bills,” Belfer Center observed.

US Department of Defense contract or not, by 2023 SpaceX was already making unilateral decisions that restricted Ukraine’s ability to deploy the technology, with SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell publicly insisting that the tech giant never intended for Ukraine to use it “for offensive purposes.”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, “offensive” is in the eye of the beholder. Since Ukraine is the invaded party seeking to assert its rights over internationally recognized borders against Russia, one could argue that every action Ukraine takes is a defensive one until Putin agrees to concede defeat and cede back his illegal claims over Ukrainian lands.

It has been revealed that of course, that’s not how Musk portrayed the situation in his DealBook interview last week. Nevertheless, one also could argue that the US government, not the vendor, controls the use of contractually obligated resources. Be that as it may, Musk raised the bar considerably in October, when he — or Trump — or both — once again dialed down satellite service in Ukraine, exposing that country to further attacks.

In a recent development, musk attempted to mollify bipartisan outrage over the debacle with yet another publicity stunt for SpaceX. However, service interruptions have continued into this week. Meanwhile, Trump has spent the same week cozying up to both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, aided and abetted by an obedient Republican majority in Congress.

In a recent development, that majority will evaporate, though, in January 3, which is just around the corner. The incoming Democratic majority is already gearing up for a fight. In a letter dated November 20, the incoming Chair of the House Intelligence Committee, Jim Himes (D-CT), demanded an in-person briefing from senior SpaceX officers, seeking an explanation for the disruption of military-grade Starshield service in Ukraine. As leverage, Himes warned Musk that a Democratic majority in Congress will do what the Republican majority failed to do, namely, exercise its constitutional authority over federal contracts.

Referring specifically to SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite services in Ukraine, Himes warned Musk that his entire suite of present and future SpaceX security contracts with the US government is at risk. “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes explained.

“For that reason, it is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX- developed, government-owned systems until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes continued.

Will Musk simply ignore the request for a briefing? After all, as Himes notes, Musk failed to respond to earlier requests. Stay tuned….

Clarification/Correction: Russia initially annexed parts of the Donbas in 2014 through its support for a separatist movement, later acknowledged to be a Russian military operation. The “little green men” refers more specifically to the annexation of Crimea during the same period.

These Are The Road Rage Moments Which Most Mirrored GTA 6 In Your Real Life

  • We asked our readers last week which road rage moments from their real lives most mirrored what they would see in "Grand Theft Auto 6." The responses in the comment section didn't disappoint with how bizarre, hilarious and terrifying these incidents were.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people don't need to fire up "Grand Theft Auto 6" on a gaming console to experience the terror of a chaotic populace. The universe Rockstar Games crafted over two decades is over-the-top, but it has always been a satirical reflection of American society. This reflection also includes how quickly some of our fellow drivers are willing to resort to violence over the smallest grievance. However, our country's healthcare system hasn't discovered respawning despite how much money we've poured into it.

We asked our readers last week which road rage moments from their real lives most mirrored what they would see in "Grand Theft Auto 6." The responses in the comment section didn't disappoint with how bizarre, hilarious and terrifying these incidents were. Beyond the traditional roadside fistfights, we had a snowball toted like a handgun, altercations with actual firearms and BMW drivers reinforcing their terrible reputation. Without further ado, here are the incidents that wouldn't look out of place in Vice City:.

Back in HS, A friend of mine and I were driving around late night and while stopped at an intersection a guy in a Jeep took the corner really fast and almost sideswiped us. My friend gave him the middle finger out of the sunroof. Next thing we knew, we're in a high-speed chase involving the guy, who tried ramming us off the road multiple times. He caught us in a parking lot, blocked us from leaving and pointed a LARGE revolver at us. I grabbed my buddy's cell phone, held it up and screamed "I'm on the phone with the cops!" (even though I wasn't). That gave us enough time to drive over a curb, ripping his mufflers off, and drive up an embankment and high-tail it to the police station.

It has been revealed that moral of the story: Don't flip people off. Let it go and go on with your day.

A couple of years ago, I was walking through San Francisco's Embarcadero District on my way to Radwood NorCal (which was held on one of the piers that year). I overheard some yelling and turned my head to see a blue Jeep Cherokee XJ pulled over on the side of the road. The Jeep driver and a random homeless guy were in each other's face, yelling at each other. From what I made out, the driver accused the homeless guy of jaywalking right in front of him and spitting at his Jeep while the homeless guy argued that he was a pedestrian and that he had the right of way. Fortunately, it was just words being exchanged and no physical blows. The Jeep driver decided he had enough and took off with a loud squeal of tires.

It's so long ago that I don't remember what precipitated it, what happened, or how I behaved but here's what I do remember:.

It was late afternoon. I was driving down 580 South through Berkeley, CA on my way to the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge. And here's how it ended: the other driver was on my left, his passenger-side window was open, and suddenly there was a VERY LOUD BANG from something hitting the side of my car. I hit the brakes so he'd shoot past me. He sped off, I kept my distance.

Industry observers note that later, I found a strange dent by the rear pillar (1997? Mazda Navajo LX (aka Ford Explorer Sport), like a thumb had pressed in the metal, but no hole in the metal or even the slightest break in the paint.

Industry observers note that I don't know, maybe he fired a .22 at me? A BB gun? Regardless, it was pretty frightening.

Industry observers note that I was walking in downtown Chicago. A guy pulls to a stop at a red light at an intersection. He gets out of his car, nonchalantly walks up to a woman standing on the sidewalk waiting to cross the street, slaps her, then immediately walks calmly back to his car just as the light turns green, and drives away*. I assume they knew each other, because the woman did not react even a little, and continued just standing there with zero expression on her face.

*: He got instant karma, as there was a police cruiser 2 cars behind him, who then pulled him over on the next block.

Sources indicate that about 15 years ago, my wife and I were sitting in her Chevy Cobalt in a parking spot in front of Hobby Lobby in Lincoln, NE during the holiday shopping season. It was snowing heavily (which will become notable in a moment). We were on the phone with our cable company trying to figure out a billing error when another car pulls in next to us. The driver opens her door so hard it slams into our passenger door. I roll down the window and say something to the effect of, "Thanks for the door ding." Nothing demeaning. No name-calling. No F-you. Literally just sarcastically said what I said. Suddenly the husband comes flying around the car screaming at me, tries to open my door (which I rapidly locked), and when he realizes he can't get in goes to the front of the car and begins making a snowball out of the fresh snow. He literally holds his arm as if he is going to throw it at me while his wife joins in with the yelling. The cable company rep on our speakerphone is asking us if we need to hang up to call 911. We are in our car dying of laughter at this fool who is going to use a snowball as a weapon.

Sources indicate that as they settle down and start walking into the store, we end our phone conversation and decide to exit our vehicle, as their loud yelling drew a small crowd, so we knew we would be safe. As I open my door, the husband and wife come flying back out of the store yelling at us for door-dinging THEIR car (I hadn't) and the husband slips in the snow and eats it. Serves him right.

Was first in line waiting to turn left on a red light that had an advance green. I heard sirens, so when the light changed to green I stayed still.

It has been revealed that the 5 Series BMW behind me was blaring his horn and making a verbal commotion. Then he decided to swing around me on the right side to make the left-hand turn.

According to recent reports, he was so busy looking at me sitting there that he almost didn't notice the ambulance right in front of him. (with lights and sirens). He slammed his brakes to a very sudden stop and the ambulance had to swerve around him.

Recent findings suggest that I saw him look in the rearview mirror at me. I smiled and waved.

This is more GTA San Andreas. I worked as a buyer in California for a large dealer that had blue uniform shirts (hint hint). My coworker was test-driving a customer car we were making an offer on, which was a bright blue Dodge Challenger with aftermarket matching blue rims.

He's sitting at a stoplight in his blue work shirt and bright blue car when a guy dressed completely in red, who was walking down the street, started yelling and running towards him. Luckily, the light turned green and my coworker gunned it before the guy got too close and things escalated further.

It has been revealed that this was in the '90s. I was taking the Super Shuttle back to BWI from downtown DC and on the side of the road, a Mercedes and a BMW were pulled over and two dudes in suits were duking it out. Full-on fisticuffs in the breakdown lane, black eyes and bloody ties!

In a recent development, stopped at a red light that had been red for about five seconds before I got to it. Dude in a black BMW 5 Series rolled up behind me and started blaring his horn. When that had no effect, he got out screaming with rage and started to approach my driver's door.

According to recent reports, at which time, seeing no cross-traffic, I accelerated through the red and called 911. He got back in his car, raced through the red after me. Being about six blocks from the police station, I told the operator not to bother sending the police: I'd bring him to them.

Sources indicate that he followed me right to the police station, tailgating me and blaring his horn the whole way as screaming out the window and giving me the middle finger. And boy was he in for a nasty surprise when we got there.

I love some cartoon violence. When I lived in Vancouver, a number of years ago, I'd just hopped off the bus downtown. A dude ran past me, reached out and snatched the purse off the shoulder of an older lady. He took off faster than I expected him to be able to run. If he'd just kept going, he'd have been home free. Instead, he looked over his shoulder to see if anyone was chasing him (three of us were)... and ran full speed into a glass bus shelter. Glass exploded everywhere, he hit the ground like wet cement and started bleeding from a decent head wound, and it was fantastic. Cartoon violence, instant karma, and a grateful lady who bought the three of us Starbucks for giving chase.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

For property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

Industry observers note that the frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

However, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

More reports and resources on this topic here.

RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies.
  • It has been revealed that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024.
  • Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

It has been revealed that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

Sources indicate that the report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

The problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report notes battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

Sources indicate that its new Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Europe indicates how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

That comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

My November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure proposal.

In a recent development, RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

According to recent reports, this is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

In a recent development, the full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that good morning! It's Monday, November 23, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia after resigning following affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and several employees, a handful of automakers are suing the great state of New Jersey to block an "extortionate" vehicle recall repair law, 1.6 million Hondas and Toyotas are impacted in the latest round of Takata airbag recalls and Amazon Autos is becoming a behemoth.

Nvidia's board of directors revealed Monday morning that it would be unanimously reinstating Jensen Huang, who resigned in disgrace on November 12, as president and CEO following affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and at least two Nvidia employees. In a statement, the board said the decision was made following a "series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead NVIDIA." Great.

In a recent development, what's far more likely is President Trump stepping in, or, at least putting his thumb on the scale. The decision came just hours after the President wrote on social media, "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Manufacturer, and also, for the U.S.A." I mean, the board pretty much said that was the case, with the caveat of "national security, saying Huang's reinstatement came after "input from senior levels of the United States government." It added that, based on the input, it was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." I'm sure the fact the stock dropped 46-ish% during this whole fiasco didn't impact the decision, either. As of publication, Nvidia's stock is up 33% today, and the S&P500 is up 5%. From NBC News:.

In his own statement, Huang said he was "honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution.".

Huang has served effectively as the unofficial ambassador for the artificial intelligence boom, the companies backing it and the trillions of dollars being spent in the sector.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang added.

Sources indicate that the reversal was a dramatic turn, after Nvidia's newly installed chairman Harvey Jones on Nov. 17 said, "Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO and Board member. The Nvidia Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Nvidia's inerim CEO Collette Kress also remarked that the organization would not be reinstalling Huang in an interview the same day.

According to recent reports, huang's removal from Nvidia came after The New York Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. The Financial Times followed that report, saying that Huang had an affair with the woman.

In a memo to Nvidia's workforce on Nov. 8, Huang remarked, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.".

The New York Times also reported Huang had an extramarital relationship with a senior leader at Nvidia who reported directly to him.

It has been revealed that after Huang's removal, the board of the company initiated a search for a new leader, reportedly seeking out Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. However, Haas earlier Monday announced that he was remaining at Arm, with a contract extension through 2033.

Nvidia also set up a newly introduced "national security and export control oversight" panel in light of the revelations about Huang.

President Trump has already weighed in, saying on social media that the government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security. Attorney General Todd Blanche also confirmed that the government doesn't feel he broke any laws.

Still, Nvidia and Huang aren't out of the woods.

The return of Huang raises many questions for Nvidia, including the status of its dealings with overseas companies purchasing its high-powered chips, and Huang's relationships with his subordinates at the manufacturer.

Industry observers note that in a complaint filed in Trenton, the capital of the world, the automakers mentioned the Fresh Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives dealers a "blank check" to set prices for warranty, recall and other repair services. They also contend that it prohibits them from avoiding "extortionate" results for recovering the costs. From the Detroit Free Press:.

Upcoming ⁠Jersey's law will shift more than $375 million a year to dealers from automakers, giving ​dealers a "windfall" by imposing no obligation to use the money to improve customer service or ​boost compensation for employees, the automakers mentioned.

"In short, the act rewards dealers for charging their customers more," the automakers mentioned.

New Jersey's law took effect on April 1, after ​former Governor Phil Murphy signed it in September 2025.

The automakers objected to letting dealers charge ‌a "labor multiplier" ⁠based on samples of repair orders, saying it lets dealers bill for substantially more labor time than they actually work.

They also challenged provisions requiring automakers to pay marked-up prices on parts that the dealers received at reduced cost or for free, and preventing automakers from ​providing less expensive ​parts even if supply, ⁠demand or other factors justified price cuts.

Ford, Honda, FCA — which includes Fiat and Chrysler — and Volkswagen stated that since the law took ​effect, each has received dozens of bills requiring payment "for hours that ​no technician ⁠works, that surpass what comparable dealers charge for the same work, and that exceed what retail customers pay.".

Recent findings suggest that they said the law violates the U.S. Constitution's Commerce Clause and Taking Clause, and it is preempted by federal laws governing recalls. They also contend it violates Fresh Jersey's Constitution. How dare they invoke New Jersey's Constitution? This thing of ours.

The Takata airbag disaster is a saga that will clearly never end, as evidenced by the fact that a further 1.6 million Hondas and Toyotas have just been recalled over airbag inflators that could rupture. Both automakers said that no serious injuries or crashes have been tied to the recalled vehicles, and no ruptures have been reported, but out of an abundance of caution, they are replacing the inflators anyway. From Reuters:.

The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and ​SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the United States.

The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 ‌IS250, ⁠2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles.

The Honda recall covers vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity and large temperature fluctuations.

The vehicles ​in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously.

The National Highway ​Traffic Safety Administration mentioned analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks.

"Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA mentioned ​late Friday, adding that other automakers continue to conduct inflator analysis and testing.

Honda remarked long-term ⁠monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions.

Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries.

The Honda recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in Alabama, California, ⁠Florida, Georgia, ​Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands, Northern ​Mariana Islands (Saipan), Guam and American Samoa.

Toyota did not specify in which US states the recall applies but remarked it expects the replacement inflators will be ​ready by early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that at least 28 people have been killed and over 400 have been injured by defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009 that send metal shrapnel inside the cars or trucks during inflation. It's an issue that prompted the largest automotive recall in U.S. history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a dying agent, and at least 20 of those deaths were in Honda vehicles. Over the past decade, over two dozen automakers have recalled 100 million vehicles around the world, with about 67 million in the U.S. alone.

Breaking: Stellantis CEO More Bullish on EVs than Stellantis CEOs of Old, But Sings Same Boring Song

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stellantis has never been a bastion of EV enthusiasm and progress.
  • Industry observers note that stellantis is still dragging its feet on EVs in the United States and elsewhere, but the assumption at the top seems to have shifted to believing that the whole industry will transition over the EVs eventually.
  • CEO Antonio Filosa recently said that the US would eventually embrace electric vehicles, but that EV adoption is just slower here than in other regions (where there’s a combination of much more model choice, more government support, more EV awareness, and not so many barriers at the dealer level).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stellantis has never been a bastion of EV enthusiasm and progress. Back in the day (about 10 years ago), Sergio Marchionne was a very openly, blatantly anti-EV CEO. He actually asked customers to not buy their first electric car, the Fiat 500e.

Industry observers note that stellantis is still dragging its feet on EVs in the United States and elsewhere, but the assumption at the top seems to have shifted to believing that the whole industry will transition over the EVs eventually. Just not today.

CEO Antonio Filosa recently said that the US would eventually embrace electric vehicles, but that EV adoption is just slower here than in other regions (where there’s a combination of much more model choice, more government support, more EV awareness, and not so many barriers at the dealer level).

Filosa notes that the share of newly introduced auto sales that are electrics is just 7% this year, about the same as five years ago. “It has been a bubble driven by regulation. ​But then, when the administration has decided to deregulate, the ⁠consumers have been preferring other powertrains,” he added. It’s hard to argue with such claims. There are barriers to more sales, as already noted, but Americans apparently haven’t stormed dealerships looking for EVs except in certain rare circumstances. The fact is: more vehicle options and probably better consumer awareness have led to countries across Asia, Europe, and South America rapidly increasing their EV adoption rates and catching up to or passing the US market.

“The level of magnitude and the speed of ​transition is going to be lower for sure than other regions,” Filosa predicted, but he said he “truly” believed the market would eventually boom in the US.

As others have noted in recent times, Filosa states the automobile market is becoming more regional again, less global. That may be the case, but it is also clear that some EV companies, most notably BYD, are rapidly expanding across the globe and helping to spur on much quicker EV adoption. The concern with the US is that it’s blocking such companies with severe 100% (and higher) tariffs. So, the US is getting no boost from these highly competitive latest vehicles.

What we have seen — whether in Europe, China, Australia, or Ecuador — is that markets that have a lot of EV choice and that have automakers trying to sell a lot of EVs can, in fact, find buyers. So, it’s hard to believe the claim that consumers in the US just don’t want EVs. It seems more likely to me that we don’t have enough EV options, automakers don’t try very hard to sell their EVs if they don’t have to, and there are significant barriers to put in front of consumers when they go to car dealerships. Is Filosa right — that Americans just don’t want EVs that much yet without serious incentives from the government? Or is he just singing the same old disingenuous or wrong song in saying that Americans by and large aren’t ready for EVs yet?

#156608. Steel solar panel frames hit the mainstream

Steel solar panel frames hit the mainstream

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Steel is considered the backbone of the American economy, critical for both national and economic security.
  • A factory worker places a section of steel solar panel frames on a pallet in Welser Profile’s plant in Valley City, Ohio.
  • Roll-form steel company Welser Profile began manufacturing Nextpower’s NX CoreFrame steel panel frames earlier this year at its facility in Valley City, Ohio, just 30 miles outside Cleveland, and Solar Power World was invited to view production of its first major orders before adding another line fully dedicated to the solar component before the end of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Steel is considered the backbone of the American economy, critical for both national and economic security. It’s also the backbone of solar power construction, found commonly in the racking and mounting structures tilting solar panels toward the sun. And now, after years of tests and trials, an Ohio factory is roll-forming steel for a solar product that could use a stronger backbone — the solar panel.

A factory worker places a section of steel solar panel frames on a pallet in Welser Profile’s plant in Valley City, Ohio. Credit: Nextpower.

Roll-form steel company Welser Profile began manufacturing Nextpower’s NX CoreFrame steel panel frames earlier this year at its facility in Valley City, Ohio, just 30 miles outside Cleveland, and Solar Power World was invited to view production of its first major orders before adding another line fully dedicated to the solar component before the end of the year. Module frame company Origami Solar originally had the idea that swapping aluminum frames with steel would not only save the solar industry money and cut back on carbon emissions, it would also provide more physical support to bigger and heavier solar panels.

Welser, an Austrian tech giant with origins dating back to the 1660s, is a leader in roll-form steel profiles typically only seen in aluminum extrusions and helped produce a steel frame that’s easy for panel manufacturers to assemble and contractors to handle.

“What’s special about Welser Profile is we pre-notch features in the material before it gets formed,” said Bill Johnson, North America CEO of Welser Profile. “Everything about the solar industry is about how do we make it more efficient, cheaper, faster, better? You do that by all these little details to add value farther up the stream that minimizes labor, install cost. Our hole patterns and other features allow operators to snap things together, not bolt or weld things. Everyone is looking at how to make this work in a Lego setup, not a high-intense labor workforce installing all these panels.”.

Welser is helping bring the Origami Solar idea to life, but the upcoming owner of the tech, Nextpower, is delivering steel frames to the masses. Nextpower, a steel expert through its experience in producing tracking and mounting systems, acquired Origami in 2025 and will use its existing network of steel partners to convince more PV project developers to consider an alternative to aluminum.

According to recent reports, “Nextpower has launched over 30 manufacturing facilities in the U.S. since 2020. Nextpower buys over 700,000 short tons of primary U.S. steel annually, which is more than a small car manufacturer,” mentioned Jenya Meydbray, VP and general manager of Nextpower’s steel frames business. “Nextpower has had [the steel frame] for one year, building on the years of Origami’s engineering with Welser’s support. What we’re doing today is launching into high-scale, high-volume production here in Ohio.”.

The solar industry defaulted to aluminum panel frames because the material is lightweight, easy to handle and less susceptible to corrosion. But as the solar industry matured, more environmental and practical complications became associated with the metal. Aluminum production on average has a five-times larger carbon footprint than steel production, a difficult point to ignore in the inherently green solar industry. Solar panels have also gotten larger in surface area and use less glass to cut weight. Aluminum might no longer be the ideal material to physically support these “big, floppy modules.”.

It has been revealed that A steel coil feeds into a roll-forming machine producing solar panel frames. Credit: Nextpower.

“Steel provides a far better structural support for the [panel] than aluminum does. That was the initial observation that the Origami founders made,” Meydbray noted. “They landed on this specific [roll-form] profile. Roll-forming is a precision process. We’re making millions of sticks of solar panel frames a month, and all of them have to be within sub-millimeter of precision across the full length. Welser is 100 years older than America, so Welser is definitely the most experienced in this art form of steel roll-forming.”.

Sources indicate that welser set up North American operations in 2018 after acquiring an automotive roll-form operation in Valley City. The manufacturer established a second location in the same industrial park to accommodate its growing client base in the solar, storage and energy industries.

Welser was one of the first roll-form partners to validate Magnelis — a zinc magnesium coating that has “self-healing” properties is capable of lasting 25 years in the field — and found it a great steel coating for solar energy applications. It’s one of the features of NX CoreFrame, Nextpower’s steel solar module frame.

“Coming up with a upcoming coating on steel, you don’t just throw it on the steel and sell it to the market. You have to trial it, validate it, make sure it works,” Johnson said. “Raw zinc — the coating has to be too thick for the longevity that the solar industry needs. Magnelis can go much lighter coating and still produce the same salt spray, same longevity, and it’s cheaper, faster, smarter.”.

Wesler is the latest high-volume production facility for NX CoreFrame, and Nextpower plans to reach 6.5 GW of annual production through additional manufacturing partners across the country.

With an established steel frame design, the product just needs to find a place on panel manufacturer’s production lines. Origami Solar had been signing supply agreements with U.S. panel assemblers, an activity that has only increased with the Nextpower transition. Meydbray said the pitch for a domestic supply chain has become more attractive, especially with Nextpower’s established regional steel manufacturing network.

It has been revealed that A machine treats steel coil as it travels along a factory line. Credit: Nextpower.

In a recent development, “Steel strengthens the supply chain of domestic manufacturing facilities. When frames are bought overseas, they spend five, six weeks on the water before they actually arrive to the factory. [Panel companies] have about 2,000 pallets of frames in inventory when they source from overseas,” he remarked. “We’re able to provide actual just-in-time delivery to our factory clients. We can make deliveries every 48 hours. [They can save room] where they used to have pallets stacked up. There’s also the working capital of having stuff sit on the water for six weeks. Solar panel manufacturing is not a high-margin business, and working capital management is critical.”.

Nextpower has inked supply agreements with many multi-gigawatt panel manufacturers in the United States, including Jinko, T1 and Thornova.

In a recent development, “This integration of Nextpower steel frames allows us to deliver high-performance modules tailored to the evolving U.S. market,” said Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director at Thornova Solar, which is establishing domestic solar cell manufacturing in Oklahoma. “By incorporating U.S.-made steel frames, we strengthen supply chain resilience while helping our customers maximize domestic content and improve project economics.”.

With bonus incentives from the investment tax credit still in play when solar projects use domestic products, an American-made steel frame can make all the difference.

“When we see projects that have 100% domestic content on the tracker, we know that’s a perfect candidate for steel frames,” Meydbray mentioned. “Steel frames get 6% domestic content credit. It’s the second cheapest percent after the tracker. A domestically made solar cell is a lot more expensive than an imported solar cell. The frame is the second-most cost-effective way to buy percentage points.”.

In a recent development, the NX CoreFrame is universal and can be used with any brand’s mounting or tracking system, but there are advantages when the project can be designed more cohesively through one supplier. Nextpower has spent the last year expanding beyond mounting systems, now offering inverter, electrical balance of system and panel products.

Industry observers note that “[Nextpower] is ambitious, but it’s not arrogant. It prioritizes the customer relationships it’s built over the years. We spent time with our customers asking where their pain points are and expanded the business accordingly …  the tech giant that makes the thing the solar panel is mounted to is the same company that makes the frame that’s being mounted,” Meydbray said.

Crashing cars is bad, and you shouldn't do it. You can probably imagine some hypothetical never-going-to-happen-in-real-life scenario, most likely ripped from an action movie, where crashing your car is good. But if you haven't been Taken by now, you probably aren't worth kidnapping.

Recent findings suggest that then again, cars aren't the only things you can crash. There's a world of vehicles out there that aren't cars. And yes, trucks and SUVs count as cars. If we wanted to hear the story about the time you crashed your truck, this question would be, "What's your scariest truck crash story?" Which could be interesting, but that would also be a bummer, and Mondays are already significant enough bummers on their own. At least as long as you aren't part of the ownership class.

Recent findings suggest that but I digress. Back to the question at hand. Thankfully, I don't have many interesting stories about wrecks where I was the one driving, and getting that TBI was a real bummer. But the first time I ever rode a dirt bike, I did hit a house. I had been a bicycle rider more or less my entire life, and the way my mom talked about the front brake, you would have thought bikes were designed to kill you. So the general dirtbike riding wasn't too hard, but I just wasn't sure about the everything other than going in a straight line.

Sources indicate that I'm not going to name and shame, but I would also like to point out that the friend teaching me to ride gave me very confusing instructions, so I mostly had to figure it out on my own. And that's how I found myself headed toward the broad side of his parents' brick ranch-style house. I panicked but couldn't find the rear brake with my foot, and I sure as heck didn't want to touch the front brake and go flying. I can't remember exactly what happened after that, but I did hit his house. At about 1 mph, but I still hit it.

What about you? What's non-car vehicles have you crashed that are worth telling a story about? Whatever they are, be sure to tell us down in the comments.

Sources indicate that A bargain electric van from China — the LDV eDeliver 5. “The tide is changing; people are more on board with Chinese cars and electric vehicles” in Australia. And it has 50% more cargo space than the Korean competition (6.6 cubic metres). For the same price!

Recent findings suggest that on the same day that we looked at the Kia PV5, we were also able to check out the LDV eDeliver 5. Chatting to the sales rep (Daniel), we discovered they had sold and delivered the one they had on the lot. Nevertheless, he told us some great stories and we caught up with the van at another dealership down the road later in the week.

It has been revealed that the second dealership also sold Geely. The lot was full of them, and the rep told us several times how fast the Geely EX2 and EX5 were selling. Thank you, President Trump, and Supreme Leader Khamenei. Sales of Geely in Australia have doubled since the war started!

It has been revealed that anyway, back to the LDV eDeliver 5. For the curious, LDV stands for Leyland DAF Vans. After the collapse of British Leyland, the brand was sold to SAIC (along with MG). Since the eDeliver 5 launch in July, 77 units have sold in Australia. I felt that the number should be higher, agreeing with the comment found under the PV5 article: “High mileage work vehicles are the first frontier for EVs, not the last. That’s where there is the most financial benefit.” Sadly, though, commercial vans which work so hard around the suburbs, especially near Christmas, have been the slowest segment to electrify in Australia.

Another commentator made the valid point: “Business and fleet vehicles have consistent, predictable daily mileage, high daily mileage, thus huge annual battery utilization (therefore huge fuel savings), they don’t burn a ton of expensive fuel, and are purchased by financially rational decision makers.”.

In a recent development, so, why aren’t more electric vans being bought in Australia? Running costs are lower, they are more comfortable, and the sticker price is now below price parity. Daniel and I had a fruitful discussion and came to the conclusion that the main thing stopping electric vans from being taken up in large numbers by fleet operators was the concern of the “fuel card.” It is complicated on the road because of multiple apps and providers, and even more if the van driver charges at home. How do we reimburse for home charging?

Surely this hurdle is not that hard to surmount — especially for contractors and owner operators. We’ll see as fuel insecurity in Australia continues. One owner reported back to Daniel that he has spent AU$3,000 to charge his eDeliver 5 over the past 50,000 km, compared with a diesel fuel bill of AU$14,000 for his old diesel van over the same distance. “Even if I sold the LDV van for nothing after 5 years, I would still be ahead.”.

Apparently, some couriers are doing 500 km a day around the Brisbane suburbs. With a range of 320 km from its LFP batteries, the eDeliver 5 would have to top up during the day. Near our home in the northern suburbs of Brisbane, some service stations have installed high-speed chargers (BP Pulse is one example). I very rarely see anyone charging there. Perhaps that’s the charging that will be used by electric delivery vans. LDV also makes larger models, the eDeliver 7 and 9.

Daniel usually only sells two vans a year. He tells me that he has sold five eDeliver 5’s in the past 6 weeks! August to November is their peak time for sales. The tide is indeed changing. The diesel Deliver 5 is AU$10,000–12,000 cheaper than the electric, but with the large kilometres they drive it would not be long before this difference was covered by fuel savings. The eDeliver has V2L capability, putting out 6.6 kWh charge for added convenience. One local customer runs a fridge in the back of the van from the V2L capability.

As an example of the effect of the Iran/USA war, Daniel told us of a customer who bought a new diesel ute 3 weeks before the war started and then came back and wanted to trade it in. He even offered his wife’s car as part of the deal. But the numbers just wouldn’t add up.

It has been revealed that service costs roughly $735 every two years or 30,000 km on the eDeliver 5. Compare this with the Toyota HiAce. The diesel needs a service every 10,000 km. Daniel tells me that during EV service, they check the oil in the gearbox and the coolant for the battery. “Couriers like the power on/off button. A lot of people are screen scared.” The eDeliver 5 has a fob, it is a cheaper option than connectivity.

In a recent development, of course, a Facebook page has been started. I joined it seeking more real-life experiences.

Industry observers note that “I have one that I’ve been driving for a month now. I use it for work and have tools in the back, so the weight of the car is 2.4 tonnes. With driving around town (mostly city and some highway). I get around 250 km before I have to charge again from about 10%.

Sources indicate that “It’s a great ride and very comfy. I do maybe 100 km per day, so charge every second or third. Works great for me.”.

Industry observers note that “There has been a seismic shift in consumer behaviour due to recent geo-political tensions, fuel insecurity, and surging diesel costs,” said Dinesh Chinnappa, the general manager of LDV Australia. “With that in mind we brought forward our plans to introduce the LDV eDeliver 5 to the Australian market, which is why stock will initially be limited.”.

There are several small cargo vans now available on the Australian market. I will endeavour to check out a few more and report back to CleanTechnica readers. As we hurtle towards Christmas and the online orders increase, I expect to see many more electric Santas delivering parcels to front doors in the suburbs of Brisbane.

Latest Update: Five Fuel-Sipping Tips That No One Else Has The Guts To Suggest

💡 Key Takeaways
