💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference.
  • Industry observers note that recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected.
  • Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Industry observers note that recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery.

To investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

The researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, highlighted that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis.

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, said the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

"Right now we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor mentioned.

"Our study revealed physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to revision international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.".

Recent findings suggest that the findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury.

According to recent reports, for Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

But the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby stated.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.".

Industry observers note that cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby mentioned.

The research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UPDATED: Nov 20 at 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on new broker enrollments, court documents show.

According to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

In a recent development, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

According to recent reports, NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

Recent findings suggest that "Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

According to recent reports, CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency remarked it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP indicates that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

Recent findings suggest that the organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker stated in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

In a recent development, CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are right now listed as enrolled in both ACA prepares and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off.
  • That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation.
  • Industry observers note that “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:09 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

Industry observers note that “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”.

Bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, the first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to consumers and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

“Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari said.

According to recent reports, connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari mentioned.

The scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that “On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari said. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”.

In a recent development, that thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari said.

Bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he remarked: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly key as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”.

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Recent findings suggest that much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA initiative Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth remarked in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

It has been revealed that the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage looks and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

In a recent development, "The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A strategy’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The tech giant sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company stated that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the tech giant noted.

In a recent development, in addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the manufacturer said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance stated.

It has been revealed that "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans.".

Sources indicate that UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The firm stated that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

Recent findings suggest that "The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Sources indicate that based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in aims with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

It has been revealed that in a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene claims that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

Industry observers note that the use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the manufacturer, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company mentioned in the lawsuit.

It has been revealed that CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the tech giant estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 proposal year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the tech giant and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company stated in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer claims that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to blueprint payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment stated in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

Industry observers note that CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

Recent findings suggest that "Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about blueprint enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the firm noted. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in looks with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, stated that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

In a recent development, "Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment mentioned in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the firm stated.

A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates.
  • In a recent development, one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

In a recent development, one possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A newly introduced study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies.

According to recent reports, to investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

In a recent development, solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly notable.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

According to recent reports, another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals Fresh Clues to Math Difficulties.

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

Recent findings suggest that the Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

According to recent reports, however, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children.

Sources indicate that an important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes.".

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

Recent findings suggest that the findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

Sources indicate that for one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services noted late Friday that it will enhancement application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for new entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give looks greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs looks.

In addition, the agency stated it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," noted CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

Sources indicate that the proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

Industry observers note that "Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy stated in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:53 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

A multicloud strategy once meant deciding which workloads lived with which provider. Now database providers are moving into the clouds customers already use, and AI projects are raising the value of those migrations well beyond the back office.

Equifax Inc. is a case in point. The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.

Sources indicate that “Their performance optimizer is so advanced that we don’t need to tune a single query,” Singh mentioned. “Just think about that. Fifteen to 20 tickets per day turns into one to two tickets per month.”.

Singh spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how a multicloud strategy is helping Equifax cut billing database tickets. (* Disclosure below.).

According to recent reports, equifax’s global billing system runs on Oracle’s billing and revenue management software, rating and invoicing billions of transactions each month. The database behind it ran on Amazon Relational Database Service for Oracle until it hit a 65-terabyte ceiling. Oracle Autonomous AI Database on AWS, built on Exadata hardware, has room for petabytes of data inside the same cloud, as enterprise adoption accelerates. Because the application stack stayed on AWS, only the database service changed, Singh explained.

Recent findings suggest that “There is zero code writing because it is just about migrating the data from one database to another,” Singh stated. “We achieved this migration without any downtime.”.

It has been revealed that the results highlighted up rapidly after the system went live in April. Gathering database statistics on nearly 100 terabytes of data dropped from three to four days to three to four hours. After some configuration tuning, batch jobs that once handled 100 to 200 rows per transaction now process 15,000 to 30,000, according to Singh.

In a recent development, “Our rating improved almost 200% to 300%,” Singh mentioned. “We are able to close our books way before what we have been closing.”.

A sprawling 8,300-square-foot hand-hewn log home on 22 wooded acres in Greenacres, WA has hit the market for under $3 million after a $320,000 price drop.

Built with full timber walls throughout and soaring views of the Pacific Northwest skyline, the seven-bedroom estate offers total seclusion just 15 minutes from the highway.

In a recent development, “It's huge. It's a 8,300-square-foot log cabin and the architecture on this one is just stunning. It's hand-hewn logs,” says listing agent Denay Hornberger with Realty One Group Eclipse. “It’s a one-of-a-kind property and the owners added a bunch of beautiful features to it.”.

Completed in 2008, the sellers bought the place before it was completed and finished the construction.

“When they first bought it, the builder had spent too much money building it and ended up having to sell it when it was half done. They came in and finished it and added hundreds of thousands of dollars to this property to make it what it is today.” Hornberger explains, adding she lives on an adjacent property. “With the money that's been put into it, [the sellers have] an eye for detail. I mean, everything about this home has been well thought out.”.

Now the owners are listing it for $2.875 million.

Industry observers note that “The thing about a property like this is trying to figure out exactly how to price it because there are no comps to really help you decide where the price is right,” she says, adding the initial asking price was a bit high. “I think we're now right in the sweet spot of where we need to be.”.

The home has seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms with real logs visible almost everywhere.

“There are similar log cabins but they're not fully log cabins the way that [this home] is. Sometimes you have little bits of logs and then you have drywall,” Hornberger states. “Here, the logs are everywhere throughout the house and that is extremely unique to have that. You feel like you are in a log cabin in every almost every single room you're in.”.

The fact the sellers spared no expense is evident immediately.

“You walk in and your breath is just taken away. It is so beautiful and it's so grand that when you walk in, you just have to take a moment and appreciate it because the windows are huge, the logs are huge,” she indicates. “The fireplace is absolutely stunning, and then you look out the window to just woods and skyline. It's just stunning.”.

The home sits on 22-acres of land and while it seems far away from civilization, it isn’t.

“You're actually 15 minutes from the freeway and you're about 20 minutes from the mall,” Hornberger claims. “So even though you feel like you're in the middle of nowhere, you just drive a little bit and you're back in the mix of things. So, you get the best of both worlds.”.

It also epitomizes the feel of the Pacific Northwest.

In a recent development, “We have that woodsy feel. People like to wear their flannel here and we're kind of a laid-back community,” she explains. “So [the house] is taking the best of the Pacific Northwest and having that cabin-in-the-woodsy feel, which is what we're known for.”.

The amount of land makes it perfect for outdoors activities like hiking and hunting, but the house is also luxurious, meaning two types of perfect buyers.

“If you just want to be outside, it’s a perfect home for that,” Hornberger says. “I think the second perfect buyer is somebody who wants a second home... who's in a hustle and bustle all the time but really wants that getaway that they can go to several times a year, have that peace and quiet from the city, get back to nature, and then go back to their regular lives at the end of the day.”.

#156529. Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1811 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to fresh research led by Stanford Medicine.
  • The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful upcoming way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline.
  • Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to fresh research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers.".

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful upcoming way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

In a recent development, the results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," noted Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.".

Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Sources indicate that transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The latest findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

In a recent development, "There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang mentioned. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be.".

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

It has been revealed that depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

Zhang recognized that this approach could overlook important biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he stated. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.".

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

According to recent reports, the Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

They examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

The comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas highlighted greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

It has been revealed that using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance.

Industry observers note that the team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

At the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores revealed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, notable differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

People whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

Sources indicate that "We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao said. "Our model highlights comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.".

A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging.

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements highlighted some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he stated.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Industry observers note that despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Sources indicate that zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially reveals a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

According to recent reports, for example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

Importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

Industry observers note that "But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he stated. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.".

Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially key new direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure organization, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

The option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

The patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is new is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

Industry observers note that “AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

In the new interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

From there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

A latest fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising new way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
  • The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.
  • Recent findings suggest that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising new way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

Recent findings suggest that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health.

It has been revealed that people with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

Recent findings suggest that "For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan mentioned.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.".

The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

Psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

Recent findings suggest that ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

"Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan noted.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.".

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety.

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine said.

According to recent reports, "The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.".

Alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A Fresh Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen said.

In a recent development, "Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an vital step forward.".

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward new dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

The ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most notable open question in mathematics.
  • Levent Alpöge announced his discovery today on his personal website.
  • “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:28 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most notable open question in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge announced his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The manufacturer floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”.

The Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects.

The Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral.

In a recent development, the Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½.

According to recent reports, the hypothesis is considered to be the most important open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern.

Another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well.

Alpöge wrote that Claude proved not only the standard version of the Riemann hypothesis but also the so-called generalized variant. The latter conjecture argues that the Riemann hypothesis holds true for not only the Riemann zeta function but also certain other, similar functions. Alpöge believes that Claude will be capable of proving an even broader version of the hypothesis in the future.

The researcher detailed that Claude’s proof runs for more than 250,000 pages. He has not yet released the paper. He did, however, publish a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used to verify mathematical results. The file contains millions of lines of code.

Sources indicate that proofs implemented in Lean are essentially regular software programs. If a Lean program runs without crashing, the mathematical argument that it describes is correct. That makes it easier for mathematicians to verify newly published proofs.
