Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Loneliness and social isolation often show up in the exam room through an older patient’s high blood pressure, worsening depression or recent emergency department visit.

Lack of social connection is an increasingly common risk factor for both physical and mental health conditions that clinicians often recognize—but may not feel well-equipped to treat.

Approximately one in four older Americans is socially isolated, and more than four in 10 report feeling lonely. Both are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, including elevated risks of heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline and dementia. Social isolation is also associated with an additional $6.7 billion in Medicare spending, mainly from avoidable hospital and nursing home utilization.

As leaders of foundations committed to improving the health and well-being of older adults, we invest heavily in programs that foster social connection, especially for underserved populations. But to truly address this public health epidemic, healthcare providers must be part of the solution.

Recent findings suggest that clinicians can play an essential role in identifying lonely and isolated patients and referring them to resources that promote social engagement. Integrating social prescribing into clinical workflows presents challenges in the current U.S. payment system, but promising approaches are showing success and can be replicated.

Sources indicate that food as Medicine (FAM) programs have already expanded our understanding of what a prescription can encompass. While physicians regularly recommend that patients adopt a healthy diet, that advice is rarely heeded for both behavioral and socioeconomic reasons. What has made a difference is a clinician’s prescribing of free or affordable individualized interventions in partnership with community-based resources and with systemwide support.

It has been revealed that similarly, social prescribing is a structured, team-based intervention that involves assessing and addressing loneliness and social isolation as part of a patient’s care plan. Taking the patient’s individualized needs and circumstances into account, a referral is made to a community organization or program that fosters social connections. These activities can range from in-person group programs to virtual activities or telephone-based companionship for people with mobility or transportation barriers.

In the United Kingdom (U.K.), Canada and Australia, established social prescribing programs have been linked to reductions in emergency department visits, hospitalizations and healthcare spending.

Brief, validated assessment tools, such as the UCLA-3-Item Loneliness Scale and the condensed Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, can be incorporated into the routine patient health questionnaires to help identify those at risk. Hospitals have a new incentive to use these screens with the recently implemented Age-Friendly Hospital Measure from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which includes addressing social vulnerability as one of five required domains.

According to recent reports, but what then? Identifying suitable programs, partnering with local organizations, and making those connections for patients is a job in itself, one that clinicians cannot reasonably be expected to add to their already full workload. And this is especially complicated in rural areas where both clinicians and programs are more likely to be limited.

Sources indicate that in the U.K., they have designated “link workers” to fill this role. Here in the U.S., value-based care team practices, which are becoming more common, can support a similar position or share those responsibilities among team members. A Social Prescribing Learning Hub from Social Prescribing USA offers practical guidance for how providers can get started, including choosing community partners and models, measuring impact and navigating the insurance landscape.

Recent findings suggest that the state of Connecticut has taken a different approach by building a social prescribing infrastructure in collaboration with SocialRx, a tech giant that matches patients with appropriate programs, enabling healthcare providers to prescribe participation in arts and cultural activities that are free to state residents. Other states, including Georgia, Massachusetts and California, have developed similar social prescribing ecosystems.

Industry observers note that some insurers and care providers are creating their own social connection programs. BCBS of Massachusetts has partnered with Elder Services of Worcester Area to reduce emergency department utilization among their Medicare Advantage members by providing Transition Coaches after hospitalizations or ED visits. The coaches screen patients for isolation and loneliness, connect them with social groups and companion visits, and help them use technology to stay connected with family, friends and healthcare providers.

Building a sustainable social prescribing infrastructure also requires government and philanthropic support for evidence-based programs that foster social connections in spaces where older adults commonly gather. One example is the American Library Association’s Aging Together initiative, supported by The John A. Hartford Foundation, which strengthens public library programs that reduce social isolation and promote older adults' health and well-being.

Other countries’ experience with social prescribing is building evidence of its effectiveness in improving social connectedness and health outcomes, as shown in a recently released evidence roundup from the Center for Health Care Strategies. However, more research is needed on how to implement effective social prescribing practices in the U.S. One such effort is a partnership between the Humana Foundation and the Aspen Institute to evaluate the prescribing, dosage and follow-up of relationship-building volunteer activities for diverse, underserved older adults who screen for loneliness or social isolation.

There is growing recognition of loneliness and social isolation as clinical risk factors impacting older adults’ health, independence and quality of life. Health professionals can play an essential role in identifying these risk factors and making social engagement a part of patients’ care intends. Support from health systems, philanthropy and the government is needed to staff and train teams, identify effective engagement strategies, build community partnerships, and establish pathways for referrals and follow-up. Working together, healthcare and community organizations can make social prescribing a practical component of age-friendly, whole-person care.

Tiffany Benjamin is CEO of the Humana Foundation. Rani E. Snyder is President of The John A. Hartford Foundation.

Hartford Foundation provides support to the American Library Association Aging Together initiative, the Social Prescribing USA Learning Hub, and the Center for Health Care Strategies' evidence roundup.

#156515. Breaking: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1683 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

In a recent development, the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely upcoming type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

Sources indicate that "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," stated Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Sources indicate that immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer mentioned. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

Doctors presently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

In a recent development, "In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

According to recent reports, "Good AI starts with good data," mentioned Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

In a recent development, "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer remarked. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a major return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Industry observers note that rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to upcoming insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a newly introduced way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer remarked, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

And it has tripled referral intakes, helped organizations book "significantly more" appointments and reduce documentation times by 90% per case.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2014, the manufacturer builds software solutions to unify enterprise data and applies AI to automate manual tasks and streamline workflows for payers and providers. As of May, it notes it serves more than 200 health systems and payers, 80 million patients across the U.S. and 95% of community pharmacies.

The Grok integration is now live for customers.

The platform plans to integrate other Grok models via API in the future, executives say, including Grok Build and Grok Bot.

Breaking: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age.
  • Sources indicate that researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years.
  • "Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Sources indicate that researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early.".

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping.

According to recent reports, daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Rolled out in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk.

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

In a recent development, one of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline.".

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding.

Recent findings suggest that authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Sources indicate that hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Industry observers note that gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

In a recent development, gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest masterplanned community in the heart of Palm Beach County's equestrian country has opened sales to wealthy horse lovers.
  • The Wellington, a private club community in the Village of Wellington, sitting about 16 miles east of West Palm Beach, will cater to the horsey set.
  • It has been revealed that the 253-unit masterplanned community—with estate homes starting at $11 million and townhomes at $6.8 million—will also feature an 18-hole link-style championship golf course designed by Scottish golf course architect David McLay Kidd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest masterplanned community in the heart of Palm Beach County's equestrian country has opened sales to wealthy horse lovers.

The Wellington, a private club community in the Village of Wellington, sitting about 16 miles east of West Palm Beach, will cater to the horsey set.

It has been revealed that the 253-unit masterplanned community—with estate homes starting at $11 million and townhomes at $6.8 million—will also feature an 18-hole link-style championship golf course designed by Scottish golf course architect David McLay Kidd. The median list price in the surrounding area is $849,900, a 12% increase over last year.

But the fresh community will distinguish itself from the luxury development pack with high-end equestrian villas and farm lots, along with a bridle path connecting to the premiere equestrian venue, Wellington International Showgrounds.

Developer Wellington Lifestyle Partners poured capital into improving the show grounds, adding 100 acres and erecting new competition rings, a covered riding arena, a grass derby field, and stabling that's designed to prioritize ventilation, horse welfare, and rider comfort.

The improvements are expected to encourage exhibitors to arrive earlier in the fall and stay longer into the spring and summer, reinforcing the village's equestrian ecosystem, which pumps about $600 million annually into the local economy, according to the county.

The 400-acre gated community, which won't be fully completed for at least seven years, has four major sections—North, South, Golf Course, and Marketplace.

It has been revealed that the first phase of the project has 49 completed estate homes on lots up to an acre, and sales began in September. (The full build-out is expected by early 2029.).

Home styles are divided into modern, transitional, and classical, with some homes offering waterfront views of football-field-sized human-made lakes.

Estates range from four to eight bedrooms, with each estate boasting a private pool and landscaped grounds. With designs by architects D. Stanley Dixon, Geoffrey Mouen Architects, Morris Adjmi Architects, and Squire & Partners, the community will be managed by Nexus Luxury Collection.

The second phase of the development, Wellington South, will have approximately 100 homes on 175 acres, with five small farms featuring a barn and paddocks.

"These will be very coveted because they will be close to the show grounds," Douglas McMahon, CEO of Wellington Lifestyle Partners and senior managing partner of Nexus Luxury Collection, tells Realtor.com®.

In a recent development, "So much of Wellington is, 'How close do you live to the show grounds?' That's desirable. Almost how you think about a ski town, people want to live near the ski mountain.".

The south portion of the development will have top-notch equestrian facilities, including competition rings, a stadium ring, a derby field, and a covered arena, as well as hundreds of stables. (There are thousands of stables and barns in the greater Wellington village and Palm Beach County.).

Beyond the home estates, there will also be 47 two-story townhomes with private back gardens and swimming pools, in addition to mudrooms for "equestrians and their gear.".

The community's amenity suite will feature private dining; resort-style pools; a fitness center with racquet campus offering tennis, padel, and pickleball; a Purple Dragon club for children; and a main clubhouse and a separate golf clubhouse.

Sources indicate that HOA fees are about $1,250 a month, plus $35,000 in annual dues for both clubs for a family. (You do not have to join the clubs.) Like most private clubs, membership is by invitation only.

"We meet everybody," indicates McMahon. "But we have one rule: Be respectful of everyone and everything.".

Incorporated in 1995, the Village of Wellington, also known as "The Winter Equestrian Capital of the World," is one of the most famed equestrian enclaves in the world.

Recent findings suggest that with nearly half of its 20,000 acres zoned for equestrian pursuits, the area contains over 100 miles of public and private bridle trails, 70 polo fields, and venues for dressage (orchestrated routines set to music) and hunter/jumper activities. There are also 800 noncompetitive farms.

"If you look at Wellington," says McMahon. "It's really a tale of two communities.".

Industry observers note that there is the year-round community of around 23,000 households; then there is the winter equestrian community stretching from January to mid-April. This swells the local population with about 500,000 spectators and 15,000 horses, flown and trucked in from around the world, and 8,000 riders representing 55 countries.

Industry observers note that it's this passionate, horse-loving audience that the development expects to attract to its new gated haven. But the developer stresses that The Wellington will appeal to others as well—such as residents who may prefer a round of golf or game of padel.

"People might want to cheer their mom or sister on [in horse pursuits], but when they're not doing that, they have other things to do," McMahon says. "We're appealing to the whole household, whether you're equestrian or not.".

While commercial activity is severely restricted within the equestrian zoning overlay, just outside of it, the fresh community will offer an 18-acre marketplace with an 80-room luxury boutique hotel and plenty of retail and office space.

It has been revealed that "Nothing wrong with a shopping center, but we're trying to create something with more feeling," the developer says. "Something with a sense of place and purpose.".

The marketplace area will also eventually house 89 residential condos at significantly lower prices than the rest of the community.

The Wellington isn't the only major development happening within the village—billionaire real estate developer Steve Ross is in the midst of building a K-12 school and a 33-acre mixed-used site.

While many buyers within the community will have homes elsewhere, coming down mostly to participate in the horse season, McMahon states that since the COVID-19 pandemic, the area sees just as many people making the enclave their primary home.

Industry observers note that "Once one is a horse family, it becomes a big part of the family's life," he adds. "The Wellington is our attempt to create a idealized version of the wonderful lifestyle that is unique and historic in Wellington.".

How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physician burnout may be falling nationally, but healthcare leaders are noting a potential latest source of overwhelm: messaging overload.
  • Leaders at Ochsner Health, per the American Medical Association (AMA), found female physicians receive about 30% more staff messages and 30% more patient messages than their male counterparts through an analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Physician burnout may be falling nationally, but healthcare leaders are noting a potential latest source of overwhelm: messaging overload.

And, it’s not affecting all providers equally.

Leaders at Ochsner Health, per the American Medical Association (AMA), found female physicians receive about 30% more staff messages and 30% more patient messages than their male counterparts through an analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data.

Though the direct causes are unknown, TigerConnect Chief Growth Officer Sheeza Hussain mentioned general messaging overload is a “symptom of a coordination problem.”.

“Healthcare slows down when people are waiting for information, decisions, consults, transfers, and discharges and all the handoffs in between,” Hussain stated. “At TigerConnect, we focus on helping health systems remove those bottlenecks by connecting people, systems and workflows so communication moves care forward.”.

Hussain continued, “When communication is orchestrated well, clinicians can focus on care, and patients can move through their care journey more smoothly and effectively.”.

Hussain and Nikki Manuel, TigerConnect clinical solution design director, spoke with Fierce Healthcare about the factors driving this trend, impacts on patient experience and how health systems can mitigate it.

Editor’s note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

Fierce Healthcare: Why does message overload land unevenly in hospitals and health systems?

According to recent reports, nikki Manuel: Nurses are at the center of patient care and care coordination, so a significant share of the communication burden often falls on them. Think about a nurse trying to reach the right provider about a change in a patient’s condition. They may need to review the EHR, confirm who is on call, determine the preferred communication method and follow up if there is no response—all while managing other patients. The burden grows when communication crosses departments or shifts and ownership is unclear. The clinicians coordinating those handoffs can end up spending valuable time navigating the communication process instead of moving more swiftly to the next step in care.

Industry observers note that sheeza Hussain: In my conversations with health system leaders, it comes back to fragmentation. Healthcare has never lacked technology, but more technology hasn’t created more connected care. Hospitals run single-purpose communication tools, fleets of devices, and disconnected biomedical equipment putting out huge volumes of alerts and alarms. None of it coordinates, which puts clinicians in the role of middleware. It’s not a tool shortage. It’s a coordination problem.

FH: As this trend takes shape, who are the clinicians most affected by potential overload?

Industry observers note that hussain: Nurses, first. They’re asked to manually bridge disconnected systems and respond to alarms. Most alarms don’t need a response, but a nurse still has to hear every one to find out. Hospitalists and on-call physicians feel it too, especially when coverage isn’t clear. Clinicians should not be middleware.

FH: How, if at all, is messaging overload shaping up to be the next source of burnout for clinicians?

Industry observers note that manuel: I don’t think messaging itself is necessarily the next source of burnout. In many ways, messaging has made communication easier. As a bedside nurse, I remember relying on pagers and phone calls and having to stop what I was doing when a provider called back. Messaging gives clinicians more flexibility to communicate without constantly interrupting patient care.

The burden comes when we layer messaging onto communication processes that haven’t been standardized. Nurses are already surrounded by alerts, messages, and notifications coming from multiple systems, and they’re often the ones deciding what needs action, who needs to receive it and what to do when there isn’t a response. That’s where the cognitive load starts to build.

Health systems should be looking at where communication can be standardized and where alerts, routing and escalation can be automated. Technology should support that process by identifying the appropriate person and helping get the right information to them without requiring a nurse to manually connect every step. Nurses shouldn’t have to serve as the middleware holding the communication process together.

Sources indicate that hussain: Because it adds to a load clinicians already carry. They’re surrounded by beeps, pings, messages and alerts, and most of it does not need action. The requirement to still read these messages and make that decision adds to cognitive overload and burnout.

It’s a thousand small interruptions compounded by the need to choose which tool to use to communicate. And the risk goes beyond burnout. When people tune out the noise, a real emergency can slip past. That’s a patient safety concern.

FH: Why do some organizations not have clear communication rules?

In a recent development, manuel: Communication practices often evolve over time as organizations grow, add new technology and adapt workflows across different departments and care teams. That can naturally lead to different ways of communicating depending on the team, the workflow or even the situation. The notable thing is establishing clear communication standards and governance around those practices.

In a recent development, hussain: Many hospitals do not have clear communication rules because communication has evolved department by department and tool by tool, rather than as an enterprise-wide workflow strategy. Health systems have invested in a lot of technology, but more technology has not always translated into more coordinated care. The result is that a nurse, physician, or operator may have to decide which system to use, who to contact, how urgent the matter is and what to do if there is no response. That is a lot of operational burden being pushed onto clinicians.

Clear communication rules are important, but they also have to be supported by technology that can operationalize those rules in real time.

FH: As messaging providers has become more commonplace at health systems, some have begun to charge for the service. How has that impacted overload, if at all?

Manuel: Research has shown that charging for certain patient messages can reduce message volume, but I don’t think we can assume that fewer messages automatically translates to less burden for clinicians.

We also have to consider the potential impact on patient access. We don’t want patients hesitating to reach out with questions or concerns because they’re unsure whether they’ll be charged. From a clinical perspective, the bigger question is whether we’re reducing the work associated with managing communication. If clinicians are still sorting through unnecessary messages, tracking down information or following up on requests that weren’t routed appropriately, we haven’t really addressed the underlying burden.

Charging may influence volume, but improving how communication is managed is what can make a meaningful difference.

FH: How does message overload ultimately affect patient experience and engagement?

Industry observers note that manuel: When we talk about message overload, I think the impact on patients is really about whether communication is helping care move forward or creating additional work and delays. When information is clear, actionable, and reaches the right person at the right time, clinicians can make decisions faster, reduce unnecessary delays, and keep care moving forward. When communication becomes fragmented or creates unnecessary noise, it can have the opposite effect.

Recent findings suggest that communication is also an crucial part of patient engagement. Patients want to understand what’s happening with their care, have their questions answered, and feel involved in decisions. When communication processes work well, clinicians have more time for those meaningful interactions and to apply their clinical judgment where it’s needed most. There’s also an element of confidence and trust. Patients may not see all of the communication happening behind the scenes, but they experience the result of it. When the care team is aligned, information is consistent, and next steps are clear, patients have greater confidence in their care and a better understanding of what to expect.

FH: How can leadership change communication without disrupting patient care?

Hussain: Leadership can start by treating communication as a patient-care-affecting workflow, not just a technology or etiquette opportunity. The goal is not to slow communication down or create more rules for clinicians to remember. The goal is to make communication more reliable, so the right information reaches the right person with the right level of urgency. That requires involving frontline clinicians, understanding where delays and interruptions are happening, and then standardizing the workflows that create the most friction. Done well, this should reduce disruption because clinicians are no longer forced to manually manage every handoff, escalation, or follow-up themselves.

FH: More broadly, what can hospitals and health systems do to mitigate this overload?

Industry observers note that hussain: Hospitals and health systems need to look at overload as a coordination problem. Clinicians are receiving messages, alerts, alarms and requests from many different systems, but those systems often are not working together. The first step is understanding where volume is coming from and which communications are truly actionable. From there, organizations can clarify escalation paths, reduce duplicative tools, and route communication based on role, schedule, urgency and context. Technology can help, but only if it is designed around the workflow.

FH: How could AI or other kinds of health tech provide relief for clinicians?

Sources indicate that hussain: AI and health tech can provide relief when they are built into real clinical workflows, not layered on top of them as another tool to manage. Clinicians do not need more alerts, inboxes or systems to check. They need technology that can reduce noise, understand urgency, identify the right person, and help activate the next step without forcing nurses, physicians, or operators to manually coordinate it all.

Sources indicate that this is where communication orchestration matters. The goal, and much of the work we focus on at TigerConnect, is to help health systems move from fragmented communication to smarter, role-based workflows that reach the right person at the right time. Used well, AI can help filter low-value communication, route information more precisely and automate routine coordination so clinicians can spend less time managing the work around care and more time with patients.

Sources indicate that the digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was rolled out in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.
  • In a recent development, those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions.
  • “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

In a recent development, those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Said another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies Upcoming York Symposium:.

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

Sources indicate that “It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he remarked during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these latest forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

In a recent development, the financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

It has been revealed that “It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

It has been revealed that the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

“We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he stated during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

It has been revealed that infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

In a recent development, “We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

It has been revealed that “You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he noted during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

“What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole company. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

Sources indicate that alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The company’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

“We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

Keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

Sources indicate that “You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he noted during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tucked away along Pine Log Creek in Fairmount, GA, sits a nearly 71-acre historic estate that feels less like a residential listing and more like a Hollywood set.
  • Known as Yarborough Mill, the $7 million property features a restored late-1800s Queen Anne Victorian—a 4,500-square-foot former grist mill and plenty of period charm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tucked away along Pine Log Creek in Fairmount, GA, sits a nearly 71-acre historic estate that feels less like a residential listing and more like a Hollywood set.

Known as Yarborough Mill, the $7 million property features a restored late-1800s Queen Anne Victorian—a 4,500-square-foot former grist mill and plenty of period charm.

"It looks like something that belongs in 'Practical Magic'," says listing agent Logan Fitts with Mountain Sotheby's International Realty. “It is definitely the most historic property I've had the chance to work with, and with that it is just so unique.”.

The property has several structures, but the highlights are the former grist mill and a late 1800s Queen Anne Victorian.

According to recent reports, “Everything's original, but it's all been restored because it was not in perfect condition when [the sellers] bought it. It's a complete restore project and everything is true to period,” Fitts explains.

“The exterior of the main house, the colors she chose, the roof tiles, the architecture, and the landscaping. Everything there was intentional.”.

The Victorian home has some Georgian features and has five bedrooms and three full bathrooms.

It has been revealed that “It looks like it could be in The Gilded Age or something like that. There are a total of eight fireplaces in the house. There's parlors, there's dens and small living rooms, and little nooks and crannies throughout the house,” he states, adding the kitchen is updated appliance-wise, but still has character.

“[There are] stained glass windows throughout, and pressed tin ceilings throughout. It’s insanely intricate.”.

But it’s another room that caught Fitts’ eye.

“They have an old solarium on the lower level that they turned into the coolest bathroom that I've ever seen,” he claims.

Industry observers note that “You have to be in there to really see it. If you’re entertaining in the house, anyone what visits or goes to that bathroom is just totally wowed. It just it feels like you're in a solarium, but it is a bathroom.”.

This home has been the seller’s primary residence, with a three-bedroom and three-bathroom cottage for guests and others, especially during events. The seller has operated a small wedding business on the property.

Industry observers note that “She's done it herself. It has been more of a passion for her. It's a wedding venue for small groups and the guest cottage is used as a bridal suite.”.

The groom’s suite and game area are above the barn, and the 4,500-square foot former grist mill is the event space.

Fitts claims most of the wedding ceremonies happen along the waterfront along Pine Log Creek, which creates a stunning backdrop.

In a recent development, “You pull up to a gate and [after] the gate opens, you go down this long winding driveway with rows of trees and the river that winds through the entire property to your right,” he explains. “Then you turn in up the bluff a little bit, and then it kind of opens up to what you would see in the olden days, like its own little village town.”.

Recent findings suggest that an old general store and smokehouse are also on the property. Fitts indicates the sellers saw a for sale listing in the newspaper at least 15 years ago, drove up to see it, fell in love with it, and then restored it.

“I was impressed with the story behind it [and] the amount of love that went into owning the property,” he says, adding there are two kinds of buyers who would be perfect for this estate.

“It could be a visionary entrepreneur that really wants to lean into making this a hospitality-based venue, spa, bed and breakfast, a true sanctuary. There's potential for growth,” Fitts explains, adding the buyer could build other structures throughout the orchard and make the main home a gathering space.

“It could be somebody's true entrepreneurial dream or it could just be someone that truly loves historical properties that wants to preserve what is there, love it with their family or for themselves, and just cherish it for what it is.”.

#156499. Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1247 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

Sources indicate that "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," indicates Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

According to recent reports, lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

It has been revealed that in 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis notes. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

In a recent development, timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and promptly enough to synchronize the sound.

Sources indicate that the team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

Recent findings suggest that by enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

Sources indicate that the researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

It has been revealed that this possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a newly introduced way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

In a recent development, "Brain waste clearance is really key for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a manufacturer that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

It has been revealed that for now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an vital question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medical associations and providers notched a legal victory over the federal government in a court ruling vacating federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

Those restrictions would have required recipients of Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care.

It was challenged by the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (HIVMA), the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in June (see that coverage below), who argued that the policy was contrary to Congress' intent when establishing the program under law in 1991, lacked sufficient explanation and discriminated against transgender people in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.

The Nov. 19 decision from Judge William G. Young, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, prohibits the government from opposing its conditions in regard to all federal funding and permanently blocks any similar policies from being implemented by associational plaintifs' members, "which covers virtually every HIV care provider in the United States," said Lambda Legal, which acted as co-counsel for the plaintiffs.

"The ruling is a decisive and important victory for transgender people with HIV and protects the ability of physicians and other health care professionals to offer evidence-based care without political interference," Philip Bolduc, M.D., chair of HIVMA, said in a statement reacting to the decision.

Young's opinion and order opened with an acknowledgement that there are "sincere and deeply felt views" regarding transgender identity, and that the matter at question was of legal regulation rather than "the propriety of individual gender expression.".

Still, the judge concluded his opinion by writing that the administration's conditions "are based in animus, loathing and discrimination. They do not stand for justice—in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand.".

A group of medical associations and providers has filed a lawsuit challenging new federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

In a recent development, the latest requirements, issued in a recent HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity, require recipients of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care. The restrictions undermine the very intent of the program, the plaintiffs say, and violate anti-discrimination components of the Fifth Amendment.

“The Ryan White Program was created as a public health intervention to address the needs of low-income, vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have access to life-saving care,” Melanie Thompson, M.D., co-chair of a primary care guidance panel for the HIV Medicine Association, said in a press release. “It is crucial that Ryan White clinicians be allowed to continue to deliver the most scientifically appropriate treatments for all patients, including transgender individuals, without discrimination if we are to improve health outcomes for all and end the U.S. HIV epidemic.".

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit alleges (PDF) that HHS and HRSA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding their statutory authority and imposing restrictions that conflict with the Ryan White statute. The plaintiffs ask the court to block enforcement of the funding restrictions.

The case was filed by Lambda Legal and HSF Kramer on behalf of the American Academy of HIV Medicine, the HIV Medicine Association and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, plus two providers.

Industry observers note that A preliminary hearing will likely be scheduled in a few weeks. Lambda Legal is “cautiously optimistic” about the future of the case, José Abrigo, senior attorney and HIV project director at Lambda Legal, told reporters on a webinar on Thursday afternoon. He called the administration’s actions “unlawful,” and remarked gender-affirming care in this context includes all types of care, including primary care and mental healthcare.

Specifically, the HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity reads: “Discretionary awards shall not be used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate … denial by the recipient of the sex binary in humans, or the belief that sex is a chosen or mutable characteristic.”.

Industry observers note that some providers are already preemptively complying with the restrictions, Abrigo stated, particularly in Tennessee and Kentucky. It is unclear how many other providers will also stop gender-affirming care. In certain cases, it’s up to individual states or departments of health to enforce the restrictions. It’s possible that medical records could be audited and reviewed for indications of pronouns, per Thompson. “It does matter what someone’s gender and pronouns are listed as,” Thompson said on the webinar, explaining that medical records are shared between providers and help ensure affirming care.

According to recent reports, if a clinic is found to be non-compliant, the repercussions are steep, Thompson added. “The penalty for being found out is severe, and puts an entire program’s funding in jeopardy,” she noted on the webinar.

Industry observers note that forty percent of American Academy of HIV Medicine members rely on Ryan White funding, of which 40% voluntarily report providing gender-affirming medical care. For low-income trans individuals with HIV, there aren’t many alternative options, per Abrigo. They may seek care through private insurance or potentially through Medicaid, but typically the population relies on Ryan White clinics for services.

Gender-affirming care restrictions under the Trump administration have been commonplace. Over 40 hospitals have reportedly stopped some gender-affirming care services for minors in response to pressure. Last week, the Cleveland Clinic promised the Department of Justice (DOJ) to commit $2 million to detransitioning services and a “decades-long” agreement not to perform gender-affirming care on minors. Delivering most of these services is at the moment illegal for minors under Ohio state law. Last month, DOJ struck a similar deal with Texas Children’s.

Industry observers note that for months, experts have been sounding the alarm about the U.S. HIV response slipping into dangerous instability. In April, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care (IAPAC) released a data brief finding that 61% of providers have reported at least one HIV service disruption and 68% have seen operational changes such as staffing reductions, service cutbacks and program closures. This was attributed to a combination of policy decisions, funding cuts and social determinants like loss of insurance coverage.

Industry observers note that “It’s a catastrophe in the making," José M. Zúñiga, AIPAC's president and CEO, told reporters on the webinar. "It was already happening. This adds fuel.".
